speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I rise on a point of order regarding the question of freedom of speech.
This is not the same question I raised as a question of privilege on March 11, but rather a point arising from public reaction to the actions of the majority of the members on the Bill C-113 legislative committee and to the ruling on that action.
The rules in this place are interpreted by you, Mr. Speaker, acting as judge of the court of Parliament on what is or what is not allowed according to the rules of this place. Like a judge in a court, you interpret the rules set down by the legislature. It is not within your jurisdiction to change them no matter how unfair or damaging the ultimate result may be in a particular case.
As you stated in a March 31 ruling on another matter and I quote:
The Chair is constrained in what the Chair can do by the rules which this House has passed. It is not surprising that sometimes the hon. members or even the members of the public feel that the rules we have set for ourselves may in some cases be unreasonable or even worse. However, it is extremely important, I think, that the Chair be bound by those rules until the House decides to change them.
It follows then that if there is a problem with the rules, the rules must be changed. Legislatures have consistently acted to amend legislation when courts have interpreted it in such a way as to create an outcry among the people who must live under the laws and their interpretation.
This is what I am asking you to do here today, Mr. Speaker. It is clear that there is a great deal of public concern about the possibility of future committee witnesses being arbitrarily silenced by a majority of a committee who do not like what they have heard from those witnesses.
A number of editorials and columnists have spoken out against the possibility of arbitrary censorship.
This place has been under attack from many different quarters for lack of democracy and lack of relevance. Some criticisms are more valid than others. However it is vital that we as parliamentarians pay attention to the voices of the people and do the best we can to make this place work in the interest of all the people of Canada,

Agreed.

April 20, 1993
Point of Order
not just those whose views we find soothing or acceptable.
We have a section in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms which guarantees the fundamental freedoms of Canadians, including freedom of thought, belief, opinion and expression. This right is subject only to such reasonable limits prescribed by law as can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society. Freedom of speech is no less important in this place. Beauchesne's sixth edition, citation 75 states:
Freedom of speech is both the least questioned and the most fundamental right of the Member of Parliament on the floor of the House and in committee.
Beauchesne's also states in citation 109:
Witnesses before committees share the same privilege of freedom of speech as Members.
It is vital that we as parliamentarians bring our guarantees of freedom of speech into line with those enjoyed under the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Freedom of speech is not unlimited but the limits on that freedom must be very explicit. That is the state of the supreme law of Canada. The supreme law of this place should also reflect that fundamental principle. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I ask you as a parliamentarian who shares my concern for freedom of speech and respect for this place to refer this matter to the House management committee to study and recommend changes to the rules.
These changes must address the need to guarantee freedom of speech in clear and unambiguous language while balancing this right against the legitimate need for decorum and order in committees. By acting quickly and decisively on this important issue, I believe we can take a significant step toward restoring the reputation of Parliament among the people of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I believe that what the member for Timmins-Chapleau has requested that you do is to take to the House management committee a request to review the rules governing freedom of speech in committee.
I am rising on that request. We in this place have already set limits that occur for members of Parliament on what they can say.
In fact, in the presentation by the hon. member he says: "Freedom of speech is not unlimited but the limits on that freedom must be very explicit".
As you know, we in this House are bound very clearly by what we can say. Similarly, witnesses and members of committee are bound by those same rules in committee although they are under the control of committee.
I believe that the rules governing freedom of speech were appropriately applied in the instance that has caused this point of order to be raised. Any time a member of Parliament or a witness appearing before a committee levels accusations of fraud or corruption against any member of this place, that member's freedom of speech has exceeded the bounds.
I would suggest that if the member is adamant that this should be reviewed there are other methods for him to do so. I do not believe that you, Mr. Speaker, as our representative should act on my behalf to request a change. I think the rules as they stand right now are adequate.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to be very brief in my intervention in support of my colleague from the New Democratic Party. He has put forward a very fair and equitable suggestion to the House.
In listening to my learned colleague across the way, the parliamentary secretary to the government House leader, I want it to be very clear that my colleague from the New Democratic Party is not revisiting. He is not asking you to re-rule or revisit your decision of March 11. He makes that very clear.
He does raise, however, a fundamental issue of considerable importance to all members of Parliament and the public as well, which is the right of freedom of speech, including where that may not take place.
My colleague has made that argument in a very succinct intervention. He is requesting that the Chair not adjudicate negatively or affirmatively on the subject matter which is in question. That is not the remedy he seeks.
My colleague seeks to have the subject matter, which he believes to be of sufficient importance, referred to the House management committee so it can examine what the hon. member and other hon. members have to say with regard to the right of freedom of speak.
I hope that on the basis of simple fairness and equity this will in no way reflect badly on the Chamber. In fact it will reflect very favourably on the Chamber if such a subject matter can be referred to the House management committee.
I might add that this committee has representatives from all three political parties and is open to other members of Parliament who wish to participate. They may go to the committee and debate. I support my colleague in the remedy he seeks, which is to have this subject matter referred to the House management committee.

speakerposition: N.D.P. Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is important to emphasize what was just said. This is a procedural suggestion rather than a substantive one. It has to do with referring a particular matter to the Standing Committee on House Management, which is the standing committee of this House charged with looking into matters of procedure and parliamentary rules, et cetera.
Point of Order
I think this is not innocuous because that is pejorative word but I think this is harmless. We should not worry that it is simply a way of revisiting a question that is otherwise not revisitable. I do not think that is what is going on here. I think there is a truly legitimate attempt to try to get something before the Standing Committee on House Management through you that deserves to be looked at.
It is not just a question of the same limitations on freedom of speech that apply in committee applying in this House. We are not free to say anything we like here. We can say things which will bring chastisement or perhaps even more serious measures from the Chair. We can be named. We can even be thrown out of the House for things we say.
To my knowledge things are never stricken from the record here. There is a new dimension here and, Mr. Speaker, you felt the rules only permitted a certain way of dealing with the question when it came before you in the form of a previous point of order. You do not make the rules. The House makes the rules and sometimes it makes them as a result of deliberations in the Standing Committee on House Management. That is where the House deliberates as the House with respect to the rules of the House.
What could be more appropriate when there is an obvious controversy than to have that body, which is charged by the House to deal with these very matters, look at them? That is all that is before us here, I say to members on the government side. There is no judgment involved here on a previous ruling of the Speaker. There is no judgment involved here on the previous behaviour of a majority of the committee that originally gave rise to this controversy. There is no judgment involved here at all. This is simply a matter that ought to be looked at by the Standing Committee on House Management.
I think that in all fairness it is a suggestion that ought to be supported by members on both sides of the House and I hope also by Mr. Speaker, so this can be dealt with in a way that on future occasions there will be some guidance from the House on this matter.

April 20, 1993

Many of us reading the press over the last number of weeks have been struck by the number of editorials and columnists who have written about this particular act; the fact that a record was removed of something that took place in an extension of this House.
I think the important thing is that we are concerned here. We want to maintain the integrity of this institution. More than that, the public is also now asking us to take some action on this issue.
For that reason I appeal to my friends on the government side to be open to an examination and a resolution of this issue. It is not simply being called upon by those of us here. Others across the country are now looking at this institution. They are puzzled by this type of action. I think it would be in the best interest of the institution of Parliament that we resolve this. This is a suggestion of at least one way to do that.

speakerposition: Speaker pro tempore
speechtext:
First of all I want to remark that the hon. member for Timmins-Chapleau has made it very clear that in raising this point of order in the House he is not, nor do I take it that anybody else is, challenging the ruling which I had to make at least as well as I could, given the constraints under which I am operating here. I think that is accepted.
I would not ordinarily invite a question of order on a matter like this. I did not invite it but the hon. member, out of courtesy for the Chair and to this place, let me know that he wished to raise it. This was several weeks ago and I said I would hear it.
The issue of the degree to which a Speaker ought to interfere with the workings of a committee is an important issue. Obviously if every time something did not go the way some people would like in a committee they could come and ask the Speaker to intervene, the implications would be considerable. Our jurisprudence is very clear. For the most part the Speaker should be very cautious about interfering with what goes on inside a committee and for good reasons, based on experience.
The hon. member has brought forward to members on both sides of the House a matter which concerns him and clearly has concerned some others, as other members have commented.
However I am very conscious of what the hon. member for Manicouagan has just pointed out.

-It is very important that a debate such as this one, serves to resolve the matter at hand. The Speaker is not commenting on the actions or decisions of the committee.

I understand very well the concern that has been raised by the hon. member. I want to be very careful that I do not do or say anything which is going to create difficulties for the House, committees or others.
I think we have to recognize that the Standing Committee on House Management has, according to the rules we have set for ourselves, certain ongoing powers. I know that the hon. member who is chairman of the committee knows and understands this.
I am reading from the rules: "The House management committee shall include in addition to the duties set forth in Standing Order 104 and among other matters". Subparagraph (3) says: "The review of and report on the Standing Orders procedure and practice in the House and its committees".
I am bringing this to the attention of hon. members because this is an ongoing thing. It is not something that is only there as a consequence of a motion of this House. There is no need for a motion of the House.
I would hope that at the moment anyway the better course would be that hon. members on both sides, and I fully appreciate they are always concerned about our rules and about how we conduct business on behalf of all Canadians who send us here, had a discussion. At this moment I think it would be wise if discussion took place between the hon. member for Timmins-Chapleau, the hon. parliamentary secretary, the chairman of the committee, the hon. member for Ontario who has spoken here, and others. It may well be appropriate that members go to the committee and discuss it. There is no harm in that. I would prefer that we approach it that way instead of putting it to a vote of the Chamber. It is a matter that has caused some distress, we all know that.
There are two sides to the matter, and I am not going to get into that. That also has to be recognized. I think that the appropriate way to deal with it, now that it has been raised in the House, would be for members on both sides to discuss it among themselves. Perhaps they would find agreement to take the matter to the committee where a further discussion could take place.
April 20, 1993

Government Orders
I think that is better than putting it to a vote of the House. This is a matter we have to deal with among ourselves and in the most civilized way that we can. I would hope that hon. members would find that approach appropriate under the present circumstances.
I thank hon. members for their representations.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I am happy to participate in this debate and I am happy that I have an opportunity to address myself to some very substantial amendments which affect the economy of Cape Breton Island and which directly affect the people who live in that part of Canada.
The sole purpose of these substantive amendments is to stop the Government of Canada from winding up Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation and transferring its functions and staff to the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. That is the substantive purpose of all of these amendments which affect Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation.
What is Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation? It is a Crown agency of the Government of Canada, put in place by the government opposite to enhance economic development on the island of Cape Breton.
There has been a long tradition going back to the late sixties of the Government of Canada taking an active role in enhancing economic opportunities in Cape Breton. We had the establishment of the Cape Breton Development Corporation which had two divisions: a coal division which is still in existence as well as an industrial development division. It is that arm, the industrial development division, which is the focus of our debate here this morning.
In 1987 the then minister responsible for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency did away with the industrial development division of Devco. In its place he told Parliament and the people of Cape Breton: "We shall establish Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation which will take the place in all of its substance and consequences of that of the industrial development division, a new agency, set apart, situated in Cape Breton to foster economic growth".
It should be noted the then minister responsible for Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency was none other than Senator Lowell Murray who said on May 18, 1988 on page 3431 of the Senate Hansard that it was a nation building measure.
That is what it was, a nation-building measure. That is what he said. Today in 1993, when conditions are unparalleled in that part of Canada in terms of its unemployment, in terms of the lack of infrastructure which is needed for our sagging steel industry and other resources, what do we have the government doing? It is removing a nation-building measure from that part of Canada. I express with great vigour my disappointment with the procedural aspects of this debate but more important with the substance of this debate. I find it shocking. I find it despicable that the minister responsible, the federal minister for Nova Scotia, the hon. member for Central Nova, has not said one word in defence of Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation. I find it more despicable that the premier of the province, the Hon. Don Cameron, has been as silent as anyone could ever be with regard to a tool that can be used for the purposes of economic development.
April 20, 1993

We know a lot about the premier of Nova Scotia when it comes to economic developments across our province and particularly in Cape Breton.
I want the record to show that the people of my province will have an opportunity to cast their judgment with regard to Don Cameron's activities in the province and also with regard to his lack of activity when it comes to supporting economic development agencies whose sole purpose and demonstrable track record has been to enhance economic opportunities in Cape Breton.
I want the House to understand that those of us who live in eastern Canada are not looking for handouts. We do not want to go cap in hand to Ontario or to Quebec looking for money, but we are looking for fairness. In seeking fairness, there is a real role for an activist government to enhance those economic opportunities. The Government of Canada could have done that if it had maintained Enterprise Cape Breton but it has decided to do away with it.
Its argument will be, as I am sure members opposite will say, that all of the functions of Enterprise Cape Breton will now be carried out by the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. That is just not so. A few will but most will not.
I need not share with my constituents for they know where I stand and where my colleague from Cape Breton-The Sydneys stands with regard to Enterprise Cape Breton.
Let us ask ourselves these questions. If it were a nation-building measure in 1988 with unemployment in excess of 28 per cent, with young people migrating from our area at a phenomenal rate, with older workers with little if anything to return to or to refer to after having been displaced, with our steel industry sagging, our fisheries in a crisis, our coal industry having declined dramatically, our forestry without direction, is that not a crisis? Should we not want to maintain a nation-building measure to try to counter some of those difficulties? Is this act to do away with this corporation done out of a spirit of meanness by the federal minister for Nova Scotia and the premier of Nova Scotia, Don Cameron?
The assistant secretary for the Treasury Board, which my colleague from Cape Breton-The Sydneys brought to my attention, said the following about Bill C-93: "Seen in this light Bill C-93 proposes to amalgamate
Government Orders
certain programs which the government wishes to continue but which can be delivered more effectively by combining with existing organizations".
It is a modest proposal if you like from a savings perspective.
It is not being done to save money. It is not being done to amalgamate and assure effectiveness. With the greatest respect, I say to you, Mr. Speaker, and through you to members of this Chamber, it is being done for solely political reasons.
It is being done because the Premier of Nova Scotia, Don Cameron and the federal minister responsible from Central Nova have determined that area of the country has Liberal representations and therefore they will choke them off.
You may think that is a cynical view. I assure you that view is real and is shared by a vast majority of the residents of the island of Cape Breton. We will see their disdain in the provincial election which has been called. We will see demonstrable signs of their disdain when a federal election is called because they will vote against the Tory administration both provincially and federally.
I urge hon. members in this Chamber, on the basis of fairness and economic opportunity to Canadians who live in a poorer region of this country, to come to their senses, re-establish and reinstate Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Marc Robitaille (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened very carefully to what was said by the opposition House leader, who gave us a good demonstration of his talents as a public speaker. It is too bad he did not use those talents to properly inform his constituents. Perhaps I may set the record straight. All services offered by the Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation will be maintained. What we are talking about here in Bill C-93 is the administrative integration of the Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation into the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency.
Motions Nos. 1 to 20 standing in the name of the opposition House leader are dilatory, their only purpose being to waste the time of the members of this House. We saw how this strategy failed at the report stage of Bill C-63 which concerned the measures to streamline gov-

April 20, 1993
Government Orders
ernment operations announced in the February 1992 budget.
These motions propose to delete, clause by clause, part II of the bill, without offering valid alternatives. As you said Mr. Speaker, they offer no substantial changes to existing clauses. They offer no valid alternatives because there are none.
Perhaps I may take a few moments to examine the reasons for the government's decision not to eliminate the Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation but to intergrate it into the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, better known as ACOA.
Since 1988, the Atlantic region has enjoyed the benefits of the economic development programs administered by ACOA to support small and medium-sized businesses. Aware of Cape Breton's special economic development needs, the federal government provided additional programs through the Crown corporation known as the Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation.
As a Crown corporation, Enterprise Cape Breton was able to develop programs adapted to the island's changing economic conditions. With reference levels totalling nearly $10 million, the corporation has offered loans, equity participation and non-refundable grants to help various sectors of the local economy.
The corporation has always maintained a close relationship with ACOA.
As a matter of fact, the enabling legislation put the corporation under the control of the minister responsible for ACOA and stated furthermore that the president of ACOA should also be president of the corporation and chair of the board of directors.
By integrating the Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation into ACOA, the government is taking steps to streamline administration costs related to economic development assistance in Cape Breton and dispelling the confusion regarding the programs available to small and medium-sized businesses on the island. What does the opposition have against maintaining the functions and services offered by the Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation while cutting administration costs and making the programs more efficient? What can possibly be wrong with trying to improve the way these organizations are managed, save money and ultimately reduce the taxpayers' burden?
As you no doubt recall, Mr. Speaker, part II of Bill C-93, which deals with ACOA and the Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation, ensures that no aspect of the federal government's commitment to Cape Breton will be lost. So stop making the people of Cape Breton and the surrounding area believe that we are in the process of getting rid of this corporation. It is not true and it is regrettable that the opposition is once again playing petty politics for partisan and local reasons, making people feel insecure.
There are provisions calling for specific initiatives to meet the needs in Cape Breton, on top of those already available under ACOA. The proposed measures are in fact programs presently administered by the Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation. In addition, the bill transfers the functions and powers of the corporation to ACOA.
All in all this move does not eliminate any services or weaken the federal government's commitment to Cape Breton. That is probably why, unlike the hon. member who spoke earlier, Premier Cameron did not raise a fuss.
The end result of the decision will in fact be to put an end to overlap and duplication of programs. The people are fed up with us not doing what must be done to save money for all taxpayers and those who contribute to the financing of the programs. They have had it with us not making an effort to terminate and eliminate unnecessary duplication.
As the only economic development agency, ACOA's Cape Breton office will administer more efficiently the programs and services previously offered by the Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation. The full integration of the corporation in the ACOA network will make it easier for the Cape Breton business community to access the full range of programs and services offered by the agency. What can the opposition possibly have against that?
My colleagues on the other side of this House are perfectly aware of the benefits of such an initiative and they have nothing better to oppose it than these filibustering tactics to waste our time. The next thing you know they will complain that they do not have enough time to debate NAFTA, the North American free trade agreement. They will complain about never being allowed enough time to debate. Just look at what they are doing today to make us waste our time.
April 20, 1993

Mr. Speaker, let me remind you also that in the documents tabled with the federal budget on February 25, 1992 the Minister of Finance stated that the Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation was in essence the local expression of the expanded mandate of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. In order to eliminate overlap and duplication and to streamline administration the Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation will not be eliminated but rather merged with ACOA. This merger will thus save the taxpayers the administrative costs of two very similar programs offered by two separate federal agencies.
Finally, the services remain, nothing has changed, but instead of having two entities there will be only one. So there will be less space to rent and lower administrative costs. What can the opposition have against trying to save public funds?
In merging these two organizations, the minister responsible for ACOA urged his departmental officials to preserve the strong points of the Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation and maintain the flexibility of its programs.
Bill C-93, I repeat, seeks to maintain the programs of the Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation through ACOA in Cape Breton.
Let us recognize these motions for what they really are: delaying tactics with no other purpose than to slow down government business and disappoint the citizens of this country who have urged us to act and told us that they have enough of waste, mismanagement and duplication and demand that we do something. We are doing something and I find it unfortunate that again the opposition shows no sensitivity in managing public funds.
Therefore I ask all members of this House to join us in rejecting these futile proposals.

Mr. Speaker, I too would like to speak on this bill.
Government Orders
I cannot believe the insensitivity of the government and the misinformation of the member for Terrebonne. He stood before the House presenting this legislation and did not even know it is not the Cape Breton Development Corporation that ACOA is going to take over, but Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation. We lost the industrial division of the Cape Breton Development Corporation before the last election five years ago. The government assured us through its spokesperson in the Senate, Senator Murray and the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond that everything would be fine in Cape Breton. Senator Murray said this was a nationbuilding measure.
I want to tell you how nation building this has been. Today in Cape Breton the unemployment rate, as reported by the government's own propaganda agency, Statistics Canada, stands at 29.4 per cent. You know that is not going to be the maximum.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, for your benefit and the benefit of the member and the House, I want to make clear that throughout my statement, I spoke of the Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation and not Devco. I think there has been an error in translation here in the House. Throughout my speech, I referred to the Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation and ACOA. I made no reference to what the member is saying.

Mr. Speaker, if that is what the hon. member stated I will accept it. Certainly that must have been a mistake in the translation.
I want to refer to what the hon. member for Terrebonne said. He said this is merely an administrative change; a money saving operation. That is not true.
The fact is that the economy on Cape Breton Island is in a devastating situation. As I mentioned, the unemployment rate right now as stated by Statistics Canada is 29.4 per cent.
I want to refer to one section of this bill. That is subclause 18(b) where it states that we are now going to, and I quote:-

April 20, 1993
Government Orders
-promote and assist, either alone or in conjunction with any person or the Government of Nova Scotia or any agency of the Government, the financing and development of industry on Cape Breton Island to provide employment outside the coal producing industry and to broaden the base of the economy of Cape Breton Island.
Mr. Speaker, I want to tell you about the Government of Nova Scotia. Since 1978 there has not been one industry established on Cape Breton Island with the help of the Government of Nova Scotia or by the Government of Nova Scotia on its own. It has not done one thing on Cape Breton Island.
Not only that, but if you were to travel to Cape Breton Island and stop at a tourist bureau on the mainland, one of the remarks you may get is "well, you do not really need to go to Cape Breton Island". In fact, the minister of tourism for Nova Scotia a few years ago, who was a cabinet minister on Cape Breton Island, had responsibility for a federal-provincial agreement on tourism, of which $14 million was to be applied to the mainland of Nova Scotia and $14 million to Cape Breton Island. This Cape Breton minister in the Nova Scotia government spent the $14 million allotted for the mainland of Nova Scotia on the mainland of Nova Scotia, but the $14 million allotted for Cape Breton he sent back to Ottawa. Imagine that. That is the co-operation we have been getting from this Government of Nova Scotia. We are being asked in this House to throw our lot in with those desperadoes. Come on. The only hope we have is that this government is going to lose the provincial election. Otherwise, it is going to be more of the same.
I will give another example. We have a university on Cape Breton Island of which we are very proud. It is in the constituency of the member for Cape Breton-East Richmond. It is one of the hopes of bolstering the economy of Cape Breton. We are dependant on the innovation that we can get through this university. I want to say that the average student allotment by the province of Nova Scotia to the University College of Cape Breton is $4,300. The average in Nova Scotia is $6,800. Even if we got the average on Cape Breton Island we would have an additional $4 million of assistance for the University College of Cape Breton.
This is the treatment we have been getting on Cape Breton Island. And this government is continually eroding any assistance to this area which so desperately needs
the support of its federal government. Now it is taking away the one independent agency that was left to work for Cape Breton Island. It says there is not going to be any difference, that it is going to be an improvement. That is not so. We are losing a great deal.
Let me just give one example which is all I have time to give in the time allotted. Under the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency there is no provision to own land. There was and there is at the present time under the Cape Breton agency. Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation does have the right to own land. Where is the industrial park that Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation has going to go? What is going to happen to it? The government has made absolutely no commitment or provision for that.
We have a demonstration farm on Cape Breton where we are trying to work on new agricultural methods, new agricultural procedures that are distinctive to the soil and to the climate of Cape Breton which is different from mainland Nova Scotia because mainland Nova Scotia goes north-northeast. It is colder, the soil is different and we need this demonstration farm. Because ACOA cannot own land, we cannot foresee how this demonstration farm is going to be able to be maintained. Is the federal Department of Agriculture going to take it over? No. Is the provincial Department of Agriculture going to take it over? No. What is going to happen to it?
That is another loss that is going to be factored into the doing away with Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation.
With regard to the fishing industry, there are no groundfish off northern Cape Breton. No groundfish. The fishing industry is in tatters and we are told you can wait, do not worry, the fishermen are not going to go on unemployment for a while. The fishermen in my riding are going to go on unemployment on May 1. This is April 20 and there is still no package for the fishermen on Cape Breton Island.
The steel industry is down from 3,700 people 15 years ago to 600 today. The mining industry is down from 4,200 people to about 2,000 today. The tourist industry has been reduced largely because of the GST which this government put in. The fishing industry is reduced because of a stupid fishing policy that this government brought in. In fact it now does not even care to subsidize
April 20, 1993

the fishermen it put out of business. It has been one problem after another as a result of the policy for Cape Breton.
Now this government is taking away the one distinctive agency that could do something on Cape Breton Island if it were allowed to function by this government, but obviously it is not. I ask the government to reconsider this idiotic provision in taking away Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation.

Mr. Speaker, I rise first of all in support of the amendments that have been introduced by the Liberal Party.
A lot in Bill C-93 is commendable. I think the opposition parties, both the Liberal Party and certainly my party, the New Democratic Party, have no problem at all in seeing greater efficiencies in government, in seeing government waste being reduced.
When you set about the task of reducing government waste you have to do it in an intelligent manner. You have to do it in a way that when you change agencies, when you restructure, you do it in a way that makes common sense, that uses intelligence, that involves consultation and then through a consensus process you proceed with the changes. There is much in Bill C-93 that illustrates this government has not done any of these things.
Certainly this clause that will roll Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation into the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency is a unilateral action undertaken by this government without the proper consultation with the people that these agencies are supposed to serve.
We tend to think that in this day and age the message is coming out loud and clear that this type of arbitrary bureaucratic government is not only wasteful but should be ending.
We hear members of the Conservative Party who are running for their leadership talk and proclaim about a new type of democracy, a new type of open government, a government that is responsive to the needs of the people, a government that consults people.
Yet when you look at what this government is actually doing despite the lofty statements of those who aspire to
Government Orders
be the leader of this government, you know that it is business as usual.
The government claims that with this measure we are going to save jobs, that it is going to make things more efficient. We heard the spokesman for the government loudly proclaim this fact and accuse the opposition of stalling, of being opposed to these measures that would cut government waste.
The government and the government spokesperson does not understand, does not hear what we are saying. We are saying that this measure will not achieve greater efficiencies. It would not reduce the deficit of this government. That is what we are trying to hammer home to this government, that what it is doing in several of the clauses of Bill C-93 is the very opposite to the aim and the lofty purpose that it proposes in this House.
For example, under the access to information the Canadian Federation of the Humanities obtained the study by Treasury Board as to the savings of items recommended under Bill C-93. We looked at Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation and what the savings will be. Over five years it will be minus $1 million. In other words, it is not going to save. It is going to cost $1 million over five years.
How many personnel reductions will there be? There will be 24 less person-years over a five-year period. It will mean that in the year 1993-94 six positions will be saved, which is true for the next four years. In a five-year period it is going to cost an extra $1 million to do the transfer and in the end it is going to save 24 positions. That again is over five years. That is the best case scenario in terms of savings.
Therefore, when this government stands up and says it is doing this to save the taxpayers money and to increase efficiencies in government, the fact of the matter is that is not so. It is smoke and mirrors that this government is introducing to us.
Let us remember that the Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation was established in 1987 by separating the industrial division of the Cape Breton Development Corporation from the coal division of the Crown corporation. At that time we were opposed to the measure. We were opposed because prior to that the focus for

April 20, 1993
Government Orders
economic development in Cape Breton was an integrated form. The general economic development as well as the economic development for coal were brought together. We sensed in our opposition that we needed an integrated approach in order to focus on the tremendous problems of Cape Breton.
At that time the government justified its action by saying this would create again "greater efficiencies". Let us have a look at the record. In March of this year Cape Breton Island had an unemployment level of some 29.4 per cent. Indeed only 33.9 per cent of the adult population had some kind of job at all.
Let us compare that with 1987 before the government attempted to make things more efficient. When the corporation was created the unemployment rate in Cape Breton Island was only 19.3 per cent with a participation rate of some 54 per cent. That is quite an accomplishment to drive up the unemployment rate to 29.4 per cent from 19.3 per cent in 1987.
When we look at the projects that have been funded under the regime this government introduced in 1987, what do we find? A report in 1991 on Enterprise Cape Breton found that those projects which had a total cost of $1 million or more had a failure rate of some 71 per cent. Enterprise Cape Breton was a participant in a number of spectacular fiascos on the island, everything from Technitread, which was a $2.1 million loss, to WCN Communications which was a $4.1 million loss.
The study also indicates, and this is very important-I think there is a lesson to be learned in this-those projects costing less than $100,000 had a success rate of 72 per cent which states that those smaller efforts at economic development had a much better chance of succeeding.
We opposed the separation of the industrial division of Devco in 1987 and we are opposed to having the corporation rolled into ACOA today. In 1988 we proposed an amendment to the legislation creating the corporation and ACOA which would have required that after two years-that is in 1990-a review would have been undertaken by the Standing Committee on Industry, Science and Technology to determine whether separating the industrial division from Devco had been a success or failure. Unfortunately at that time the government opposed the amendment.
.(1135)
We have heard the government spokesperson talk about the opposition being motivated mainly by political considerations. That is not true. We want to see an effective program. That is why in 1988 we introduced amendments to ensure that there would be a proper review of what Parliament had done in 1988.
The government could have accepted our proposal instead of playing politics. However because the suggestion came from the opposition the government automatically, in a knee-jerk reaction, opposed it. It could have accepted our amendment as a well-intentioned amendment aimed at allowing a review after two years to make certain that what we had done in 1988 was the correct thing, and if it was not, to allow us an opportunity to redirect and correct any mistakes we made. No, the government was opposed.
In the absence of any other alternative a full review of the success or failure of that amalgamation should have preceded the abandonment of that corporation and the rolling of its activities into ACOA. What we are asking for is a proper review.
The government is saying that we are wasting time. Is it a waste of time to make certain that the review is done right so that moneys can be saved, so that the purpose of this exercise, economic development on Cape Breton, can be done in the most efficient way? That is what we are trying to do and what we are trying to seek.
We are not trying to score political points. We want to make certain that what we do as a public body we do in the best way.
What it comes down to is local control. The people of Cape Breton Island should really have ultimate control over their destiny and economic development. They are the people who know the best. What the government is doing today is taking control further away from them. It is a pigheaded and stupid move on behalf of this government that makes no sense.

speakeroldname: Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands - Canso):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak to the set of motions by my colleague, the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond, which attempt to prevent the rolling into ACOA of Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation. They attempt to preserve the single agency left on
April 20, 1993

Cape Breton Island that can plan the economic future of Cape Breton Island as a whole.
The provision in Bill C-93 to eliminate Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation can only be described, if one regards it in the historical context of this government's activities with respect to Cape Breton, as one of astonishing cynicism.
If we go back to the beginnings of this government, back in 1984-85, and examine the record of the government in terms of promoting development on Cape Breton Island we see a government that had a few ideas initially but has totally given up. It has decided that Cape Breton Island is a place where it has no support and there is no point in even investing a modicum of energy or resources in an attempt to create an economic future for that part of Canada. It has written that part of Canada off.
When Devco was created back in 1967 as a federal Crown corporation to run the coal industry in Cape Breton the industrial development division was added to Devco in order to promote alternatives to coal and steel and create a diversified economy on Cape Breton Island. We realized then and we still realize that it is a long-term, ongoing prospect. The government of the day considered Cape Breton Island as an economic entity that required a focus, a focused plan of development and a focused agency to promote the opportunities of the island and to try to find by trial and error alternative economic opportunities for the island.
In 1988 when this government took the industrial development division of Devco, broke it off from Devco and created the Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation, this party saw then that the intention of the government was ultimately to terminate that agency whose mandate and focus was to promote economic development on Cape Breton Island. We saw it in the words of the government leader in the Senate when he said in introducing Bill C-103, which was an act to create ACOA, that this was a nation building measure. Creating Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation as a separate agency from the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency was a nation building measure.
In another part of his speech he said that the purpose of this organization was to: "Promote and assist in the financing and development of industry on the island of
Government Orders
Cape Breton in order to provide employment outside the coal mining industry and to broaden the base of the economy of the island". That was what the purpose of the industrial development division was. He said that Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation would do this on its own and in conjunction with others, whether individuals, governments or government agencies.
We knew at that time that the government's ultimate plan was to eliminate the industrial development division of Devco, to eliminate a separate agency to promote economic development on Cape Breton Island and to roll it in with the rest of the hodgepodge of programs it has created and which have had no focus and no effect. The government has literally thrown money at Cape Breton and at the rest of Atlantic Canada but it has had no effect in terms of promoting some kind of focused economic development in that part of the world.
At the same time the fundamental resource based industries that we have, such as the fishery which is in a state of collapse all around our shores through no fault of the people involved in the industry but largely because of its mismanagement by this federal government and the coal and steel industries which have been struggling for generations and for which we are still striving to find some ways of providing some alternative, continue to be all that exists to sustain the people of Cape Breton, those who are willing to stay in that part of the island. We still need a focused agency to come up with alternatives and find the natural opportunities that exist in Cape Breton to create meaningful, long-term and stable employment for our citizens and our young people for the future.
The measures that have been created, the programs of loan guarantees, interest buy-downs and investment tax credits which the government has lobbed in our direction and then taken away, altered and changed at a whim and a moment's notice, have actually undermined more than anything the entrepreneurship and natural business acumen of the people of the island.
It had them chasing grants, loan guarantees and interest buy-downs. It had them chasing smoke stacks from other parts of Canada who have come with no reason to stay on the island. We have had to live with this over the whole period of this government.

April 20, 1993
Government Orders
Here we are in the dying days of a Tory administration that has lost all sense of purpose and all sense of commitment. It has no ideas and has bankrupted any solutions for this part of the country. It is taking away the only agency which, small though it was, was trying and was in a position to focus and deal with the problems unique to Cape Breton Island.
That is what this government is doing with Bill C-93. That is why the members of Parliament who represent that part of Canada are so opposed to this bill.
In 1988, just before the last election when the government created ACOA, we had a flurry of announcements of businesses starting up all over Atlantic Canada. In Cape Breton Island the people had money forced on them. Many businesses were started up prematurely. I know because they are in my riding. They gave up their life savings to set up corporations induced by these incentives given by the government just before the election. After the election the incentives disappeared and the businesses struggled on. Many of them went bankrupt.
The life savings of some of those people went with them. We had the situation of a few months ago, and I do not want to let this go by, in which Premium Automotive Tanks Inc. in Port Hawkesbury, after five years of taking this government's money and taking the talents and dreams of the people of Port Hawkesbury, closed its doors overnight.
Yesterday I discovered three employees of that company who for some reason were not on the list to get their severance payments and are being denied their severance payments by that company. Now that the company has its assets out of Port Hawkesbury it does not need to care and does not care about the employees who are there and who are trying at least to get a severance package so they can begin to rebuild their lives.
That is the legacy of this government on Cape Breton Island. That is why it knows that it will get absolutely no support provincially or federally in the next election.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be given the opportunity to talk about this series of amendments because this particular activity is
probably one of the worst initiatives that the government has ever undertaken.
It has been a botched job right from the beginning. In fact, ce sera appele I'operation malmenee.
I already have graduate students who are contacting me to do theses at the masters and doctoral levels. They want to do a case study of something that has been particularly badly done by government. This is the one that they are zeroing in on.
Why is Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation being axed? It raises very fundamental questions if it is going to be done away with, as it will be. What is next? The more important question is why did the government decide to do that?
I have maintained right from the beginning that it was to try to respond to the right wing of its party, the reform agenda. I suppose that because I am from this side of the House people might say that is what I would say. I would like the ladies and gentlemen in the House to cast their eyes on an article in The Globe and Mail from February 27, 1993 by a well-known writer by the name of Hugh Winsor.
He was interviewing a senator by the name of Finlay MacDonald, who is a senator from the government's side. While talking to him this is what the good senator had to say. He saw this whole exercise as the government's attempt to thin the public perception that chronic deficits are caused by waste and mismanagement as it allows the public to believe there is a painless way to solve our serious financial problems. That is one comment which the senator made. The other one is equally effective and I find it more interesting. The whole exercise might be nothing more than a symbolic act to protect the party's right flank from attacks from the dreaded Reform Party and cause sufficient pain and spill enough blood to impress the voters. If this is true it might be good politics in the short term but it is not good public policy in the long term.
I did not say that. Senator Finlay MacDonald said it. It is available to anyone and everyone. I would be delighted to carry it to them personally.
April 20, 1993

Let us look at the contentions that the government made. It is going to save money. I will speak to that later. It is going to increase efficiency and effectiveness. I will speak to that later.
I say to the government side that is why it is such a botched operation,

It was botchedry because no studies were ever made. Can you imagine the government introducing a bill of this magnitude, winding up some agencies and consolidating others, without any preliminary studies to determine whether it will save money or increase efficiency.

Where is the proof? Give me the proof and I will reconsider my position. I contend it was nothing but a blatant political act.
In the interest of fairness I want to quote from some of the testimony that was given by those representing the government. Bill C-93 is a modest proposal if you like from a savings perspective. In one particular case they point out that the changes will cost government additional money. Can you imagine that? That is what they say.
Let me quote again from one of the government witnesses: " But we have no particular studies on costing on the savings". When I asked where the increased effectiveness would be they said it may well be possible by putting organizations together that work well together to find better ways of delivering services in addition to the strict cost economies that are provided. Those are not estimated in the numbers, of course. That is what they have done.
I wanted to get that on the record and make sure people understand that whether we happen to be talking about Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation or the removal of the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council by consolidating it with the Canada Council, or any number of features of this particular bill, we are not talking about saving money. We are not talking about increasing efficiency or effectiveness. We are tallung raw politics.
Why am I saying that? I gave a quote and pointed out there are no studies. There will be no money saved. There will be no additional effectiveness. If the government was really serious about saving money and doing
Government Orders
something to increase efficiency and effectiveness it would have called those organizations together and told them how much it needed to save. It would have told them the effectiveness or efficiency it wanted to realize.
Did it do that? Oh, no. There are brave soldiers on the government side. We have to admit that. They sent their civil servants to the slaughter house. It was terrible. I felt very bad. In fact I went in there angiy and finally had to back off because those poor souls had been sent by those insensitive politicians on the government side. Now those elected officials on the government side are doing their best. They have been sent out of the trenches without any protection. There are no savings. There is no increased efficiency. This is a political act. The government is trying to get close to its kissing cousins, the Reformers.
I am going to wager any odds that it is not going to work. Find me one responsible person who says these are good ideas in terms of saving money and increasing effectiveness, besides elected Conservative officials who may be under tremendous pressure to do what their political masters ask them to do, and I will reconsider my position.

Mr. Speaker, speaking on behalf of the motion for the amendments that have been moved in my name, let me at the outset point out to the House that we have worked very closely with the Liberal Party as well.
The amendments that stand in my name that were dealt with in the legislative committee that considered Bill C-93 I suggest and suspect represent the feelings and the thinking of a lot of members in this House from all parties.
Basically what does it do? What my amendments ask for is that part III of Bill C-93 be dropped entirely. This is the part that attempts to fold the Social Sciences and the Humanities Research Council and the International Cultural Program into an expanded new entity consisting mainly of the Canada Council.

April 20, 1993
Government Orders
We heard in committees members of the academic community, the arts community, the research community, university administrators, the Canadian Association of University Teachers, the whole academic, research and arts community of this country totally and unanimously condemning this section of Bill C-93.
As well in committee we heard from members of the Treasury Board, the finance department and even from the PCO that there will be no savings at all in this measure. If anything it is going to cost the government money.
Here we have another example of where in the name of deficit reduction the government is actually going to increase its deficit. Here we have an instance in which the government claims it is going to increase efficiencies. We have the officials of Treasury Board, the finance department and PCO admitting that it is not going to increase efficiencies. In fact what we hear from the academic community and arts community is that it is already creating increased inefficiencies.
The attempts to bring the people who work in SSHRC and in the International Cultural Programs into the Canada Council is causing a whole host of problems. There are financial costs and personal costs. This makes no rational sense whatsoever and government members know it.
They say it is to increase efficiencies. Let us have a look. The Social Sciences and the Humanities Research Council administrative cost in 1978-79 was 13.1 per cent. Now it is 8.7 per cent. Great efficiencies.
What else does this motion do? Without any prior consultation with the academic community, the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council and other research bodies, absolutely no consultation whatsoever, a small group of bureaucrats decided that they were going to unilaterally move the clock back.
Up until 1978 the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council was part of the Canada Council. The Lamontagne committee report on sciences in this country still stands out as one of the best reports ever produced on science policy. It recommended that the Social Sciences and the Humanities Research Council be recognized as a separate entity to receive funding for research. It was important to the social sciences and to the humanities to be recognized as a body of scientific research, that it was a legitimate forum of scientific
research on its own, that it was not part of the arts but that it was a scientific research entity on its own.
When SSHRC was separated from the Canada Council it was an important and fundamental recognition for the social sciences and the humanities. This government, through the actions of a few bureaucrats, has decided that this is now not the case and it is going to roll the social sciences and the humanities right back into the Canada Council. The arrogance of it.
It is the arbitrary nature of this that is the most disturbing of all. What is happening to democracy here? In committee I kept asking why the government was doing this. I kept asking government people and bureaucrats from the departments why they were doing this. Nobody was able to come up with a rational answer in front of the committee. I suspect the government is doing it for entirely political reasons. It wants to show the right wing nuts in the Reform Party that it is macho and tough and that it is cleaning up government when in fact it is doing the opposite.
What has happened to the whole notion of rational policy making? What has happened to the whole notion of appropriate and intelligent actions? When you are attempting to reduce the deficit and increase efficiency the first step is to study the situation, consult and then take appropriate common sense actions. In this case of course none of this occurred.
In the leadership race for the Conservative Party we hear all of the contenders talk about the new type of politics, the politics of inclusion and politics that allow ordinary members of Parliament to function more independently and effectively in committee. Here is the test.
I challenge all of those leadership contenders and their supporters to stand up in this House today and vote against part III of Bill C-93 because it is not the politics of inclusion. It is arbitrary politics. It is politics that has totally upset all of the researchers and social scientists across this country for no valid reason whatsoever. There are no savings, there is no inclusion and there is of course no consultation.
If the government is going to have the new politics then let us see it demonstrate it today. Otherwise those members who talk about new politics, aspiring to be leader of their party, will demonstrate clearly that all they are talking about is a bunch of smoke and mirrors and that they have no intention arid no idea what real, new, inclusive politics is all about.
April 20, 1993

What we are finding is an abuse of power and macho politics, the worst type of politics that the people of this country are sick and tired of.
I and most Canadians assume that six months from now this group will be gone and that the arbitrariness of this government will be gone. I would suggest to all those who are responsible for implementing part III of Bill C-93 treat this as an academic theoretical exercise, that they keep track of where every desk, file, typewriter and computer comes from so that when the political reality of this country is changed in six months we can unscramble what is being done today and we can restore the Social Sciences and the Elumanities Research Council to its proper role as a separate, scientific organization administering itself on its own so that the international cultural program can again be put back in external affairs where it properly belongs. Let me advise all those who are in charge of implementing this policy that it is not going to be a policy that will last for more than six months. Both the Liberal Party and the New Democratic Party are on the record as being committed to restoring the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada and the International Cultural Program back to where they are now.
Let it be a suggestion to all those involved in implementing Bill C-98, part III, to do it with a fair amount of care and to keep track of where everything has come from so that we can unscramble this mess that this government has created in the most efficient way possible.
I make an appeal to government members who do believe in the politics of inclusion, who do believe not in arbitrary government bureaucratic action but action based on consultation and common sense, to stand up for those principles in the House and vote in favour of the amendments I have introduced today.

Mr. Speaker, I want to commend my colleague for his address that I thought to be very thoughtful and in fact very useful.
I had considered motions to rescind, which means having the whole section deleted. It may be of interest to know and I certainly will not put the finger on anyone but at one particular point in time we entered into discussions with members of the government side who understood how vulnerable they were and how badly the work had been done here. were no studies or consultation, there would not be any money saved and there would be no increased efficiency or effectiveness.
We thought there was an opening or a possibility that we might co-operatively work together to rescind that particular section of the bill. Of course what we would have done next would have been to simply look at the bill in an objective kind of way to tiy to determine if there was something worth saving.
I was hopeful on that particular day that we might have had an agreement so that we might have been able to rescind that.

I had high hopes, when I saw some members who are experts on the subject, that we would be able to rescind this section.

Unfortunately it was not possible. I deplore the fact, as do my colleagues, that there was no consultation. None. Can one imagine? We are talking about all of these national organizations that are staffed with some of the finest people in the land and that represent some of the major groups who keep this country together and make it work. There was no consultation. There were no studies to show that what the government was contending would save money. Can one imagine that? There were no studies to show increased effectiveness or efficiency. Can one imagine that?
I cannot believe that a government would be so insensitive, that it would be so gauche as they say in French.

I think that is a very apt expression. It made a monumental mistake with this bill, and it will pay a very high price for doing so. My hon. colleagues know it is too late. The government had its chance. If it had been willing to rescind this section, it would have been perceived as a government that can listen. However, because it was uncomfortable about the whole thing, it said to itself that it would go ahead, even if it was a bad bill. Well it will pay the price.

There is another point I would like to make, and I want my hon. colleagues to listen very carefully. Just try and find someone who represents these agencies, someone who has credibility, who will tell the government:

"We think that this merger is a great idea". Find one credible individual. We heard testimony from the Canadian Association of University Teachers, the Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada, social scientists and the Canada Council, et cetera. There was not one individual who thought this was a good idea.
In fact the government was so badly prepared that it was embarrassing. It was even embarrassing for me as a member of the opposition who normally likes to see the government get what it deserves, particularly when it has done a shoddy job.
It was so bad that I wanted to say to people: "Please back off". It cannot find one single person in the whole land who would say: "This is a good idea". That is how bad this project really is.
What were these people asking? Were they saying: "Stop it."? No, they were making a very reasoned response. They said: "Delay the decision. Defer that decision. You do not have to stop what you are doing if after consultation and after study you still believe that this is a good decision. However, please consult, study and reflect and then make your decision".
What an approach.

I would have thought that the government would welcome this proposal with open arms.

Therefore, that is why I am really quite disappointed today. I think my colleague's motions to rescind, obviously, would have been the best. I had hoped as I said earlier that this would have been possible. Unfortunately it is
not. The government has chosen to go forward in spite of all the evidence that this is going to go down in the history of this Parliament as one of the worst, if not the worst blunder ever made by this government.

I never thought this government would have been so shortsighted, so clumsy that it would have stumbled so badly.

Once again I want to extend a word of appreciation to those brave civil servants who went out knowing that there was nothing there to protect. They knew there was nothing there to protect.
There are the politicians who still today in spite of the evidence will stand up for the government. If nothing else, there is loyalty there.
I have to tell you, Mr. Speaker, and I think you will agree with me, that loyalty without reflection and common sense is extremely dangerous. This is what we are faced with today.

This is a bill that should be withdrawn altogether and completely revamped, instead of being pushed ahead regardless of the consequences.

I am sorry that this is happening. In fact we could all redeem ourselves if we were to say that this series of amendments makes so much sense that we are going to accept them. I see a smile on the face of one of my colleagues. We could set aside partisan politics, study this and then decide what is the right thing to do.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext:
Mr
Speaker, I welcome the oportunity to join the debate at report stage on Bill C-93.
April 20, 1993

Since the bill was reported back to the House on February 25th, the government has had the opportunity to reflect on a number of additional proposals which members opposite have put forward and has also observed the need for certain technical amendments to facilitate implementation of the bill at the appropriate time.
I will be dealing with these matters in detail in a few moments. First, Mr. Speaker, I want to deal with some of the mischief which has resulted from the efforts of my friends opposite in the legislative committee and the subsequent media coverage and editorials.
The opposition has tried, I believe, to characterize Bill C-93 as a smoke and mirrors exercise, not worth the candle from the perspective of the small savings it will generate over time. In this regard, a significant amount of their efforts and the media follow-up have been focused on part III of the bill, the proposed establishment of a reconstituted Canada Council for the arts and for research in the social sciences and the humanities.
In the legislative committee the hon. member for Mount Royal adduced a February 20, 1992 Treasury Board document dealing with forecasts of savings related to the wind-up and merger measures announced in the February 1992 budget. The reference to dollar savings for a "new single cultural agency" showed a figure of zero for 1992-93 and the four outlying years.
This document was also included in the public submission to the legislative committee from one of the cultural organizations which testified on February 22, 1992. Although officials attempted to explain that this figure merely represented the fact that no firm targets for savings here had been established, my friends opposite have been successful in persuading the press at least that the figure means that no savings would result and that the merger is therefore not a sensible idea.
It must be said that before 1974 these two bodies were combined. The government in the 1974 Speech from the Throne announced the creation of two new granting councils: the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council, separate from the Canada Council, and the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council, separate from the National Research Council.
Government Orders
It is interesting to review this development because the split between the Canada Council and SSHRC in 1978 was criticized for mostly the same reasons for which the merger is now under attack.
There were concerns about the independence of the new council, dissatisfaction with administrative costs related to the separation, anxiety over inadequate funding and nervousness about the impact on the humanities.
In fact at second reading in the other place, Senator Hicks said, and I quote: "I am very much concerned that this bill, rather than helping the problem of underfunding, will only add to the administrative costs and diminish the sums of money that may be available to carry out the purposes for which the councils are being created".
I believe he was right, since the information on hand indicate that the administrative rate of this body increased by 200 per cent between 1978 and 1992.
I would remind the House that part III of Bill C-93 proposes to consolidate three existing organizations with a combined annual appropriation for fiscal year 1993-94 of $217 million and a combined administrative overhead of about $35 million.
You will appreciate that with an undertaking of this size it is difficult to be precise in anticipating savings over four or five years. This merger is unlike that of smaller agencies in the bill where the smaller size of those entities makes it possible to be more definitive.
Nevertheless, I am pleased to advise the House today that once the transition to the new organization is complete, it will result in ongoing annual savings of about $5 million, probably as early as in the third year of operation of the new Canada Council for the arts and for research in the social sciences and humanities.
As announced by the Canada Council in its March 13, 1993 press release, the Council will be undertaking as part of its strategic planning process a comprehensive organizational and program review in order to increase administrative savings through a streamlined program structure, simpler procedures and reporting obligations and more flexible financial management primarily through the creation of a multi-year assessment and funding process.

April 20, 1993
Government Orders
In general terms, we would expect savings to result from colocation with the use of less space at lower costs, from grants awarded on a three-year basis rather than annually, from the reduced costs of the combined council and from streamlining of the financial, personnel and information systems.
There will be some technological improvements to data bases and we expect that some functions might be cheaper to perform in-house which are currently contracted out.
Allow me to comment briefly on Motion No. 40 tabled by my colleague from the opposition.
Of all these amendments to part III of Bill C-93, Motion No. 40 is the one which the government is most ready to accept the spirit of. It is desirable to provide for a review of the new council's activities after a reasonable period of transition and stabilization. On the other hand, the government believes that a mandatory legislative review of the new council by Parliament at a prescribed date in five years is not necessary. In fact, such a review might not be appropriate for the government in place then, which will have its own agenda and which will have to face the pressing issues that the future may hold.
For this reason, the government proposed instead Motion No. 38, which provides for a review during the sixth year of activity of the council. This review would be conducted by the council itself in consultation with the concerned communities and would be independent of Parliament's activities, albeit in conjunction with the latter. The results of these reviews would be presented in reports tabled before Parliament, which would follow up on these as it would please. For these reasons I sincerely hope the hon. member who tabled Motion No. 40 will take into account the government's motion and withdraw his own motion.
In conclusion, it is important to remind ourselves that we are dealing at present with an established Crown corporation and that will be the organizational form of the new council once Bill C-93 is adopted. Therefore it is not for me or for the government to tell you precisely how these savings will be realized.
Indeed it would be inappropriate for me to venture to do so if we are to respect the arm's length relationship to the government that Crown corporations enjoy. Suffice it to say, management has given us its best forecast of the prospects for savings at this early stage of the reintegration.
We on this side of the House accept that. It will be up to the board of directors and management of the new council to determine precisely how these savings will be realized. However, I do think that roughly $5 million annually is a significant amount of money to be generated from a government streamlining measure.
I hope that will put an end to the line of nonsense my friends opposite have been spouting that there are no savings to be achieved from part III of Bill C-93.
In concluding, I must deplore the fact that my colleagues from the opposition, both Liberals and New Democrats, show so little concern for a healthy management of public funds and the fact that we can make relatively important savings for Canadians who these days must make their own budgets and constantly try to make ends meet. In that context, $5 million is an important amount.

Point of order, Mr. Speaker. We just heard the government member make all sorts of claims in this House about savings. We also heard him say that the administrative costs for one of the agencies went up some 200 per cent. I heard him say this measure is going to save $6 million. Later I heard him say it is going to save $5 million. He is referring to figures and studies that we as members of Parliament do not have access to.
Is the hon. member prepared to table before this House any studies whatsoever that he or the government has that show any savings?
