Mr. Speaker, I rise to address the interesting remarks made by the parliamentary secretary. I want to thank my colleague, the member for Regina-Qu'Appelle, who noted the interesting group of figures presented in this very emotional and historical recall of the history of the Social Sciences and Humanities Council and Canada Council, forgetting the fact that when they were brought together it was not an harmonious marriage. That particular relationship could not even be saved through marriage counselling. Two mismatched organisms had been brought together, so the divorce took place. Then the forced remarriage was brought about by this government through poor rationale and reasoning. Part of that poor reasoning was the supposed saving of money.
There were never any new facts brought into those committees for which I did not have documentation. I wish I had the documentation here in the House to refute those kinds of observations as I did in committee. I was quite fascinated to see that the documents which had been received at that time through access to information did not seem to stun the bureaucrats who were in the committee at that time. If the various groups who were concerned with this particular matter reacted and accepted the materials which I tabled in committee it is because the source seemed to have been right.
They say they bought my information. I am sure the members of the Canadian Federation for the Humanities looked into it. I know that various other groups examined it very carefully. I have before me a press release from the Canadian Federation for the Humanities that was released on February 17 1993. It stated: "For a year we have been led to believe that the government's decision to collapse the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council into the Canada
Government Orders
Council had everything to do with a desire to save taxpayers' dollars. This merger, we have been told again and again, is a necessary part of the streamlining of 46 federal agencies that will net the taxpayers $22 million annually".
I talked to the few mergers that were intelligent in there, on copyright and other issues, but most of them were very poorly thought through. The first 20 amendments that were debated earlier today are a perfect example of the ACOA situation. Certainly the amendments my colleagues, the member for St. Boniface and the member for Regina-Qu'Appelle, have brought in here add to the intelligence of the need for some change.
Dr. Robert Nadeau says, and I quote: "This is ludicrous. It has become clear to us that the Canada Council merger saves us no money at all. The only saving indicated in the document dated February 20, 1992 is a minuscule 10 person-years. The government's decision to throw research in the humanities and social sciences into the chaos of wholesale reorganization for the sake of 10 person-years in our view is completely irresponsible". If the government is trying to tell me that by putting these three groups together it is going to save $5 million on 10 person-years, I would like to know what kind of salaries it is referring to.
"The deficit made us do it" is the other thing the government has been saying in its defence from the start. Now it is perfectly clear that the government embarked on the SSHRC and Canada Council merger with absolutely no concern for either real savings or real cost to the taxpayers. We already have the lean, mean machine the government says it is busy creating. It is really taking it apart. The Canadian Federation for the Humanities urges the government to excise part III of Bill C-93 presently being studied and now before the House because the merger does not save money. It is likely to waste both time and money and should not be part of this bill at all.
I remind this House that I put a motion before this House on December 4, 1992 which would have suspended this bill. It would have read that an act to implement certain government organization provisions be not read now a second time but be read a second time six months hence. That was defeated by this government. It was a votable motion and this government did not care

April 20, 1993
Government Orders
to listen. This is the government that says we must be more caring, more concerned and listen to the people. It did not consult with Canada Council. It stripped, cut and hurt Canada Council and paid no attention to the needs of the artists. It actually has shown little concern for the fact that this is one of the most fundamental organizations we have in Canada. Its financial clout has been able to develop cultural activity and growth in Canada.
I suppose that is not of interest because certainly this government's rhetoric has been displaced by the kind of cuts it has administered to Canada Council. It was not interested in the Canada Council's side and it certainly was not interested in the science and humanities research side because if it was, it would not be cutting this right now. It would be doing everything in its power to find answers to what is going on in Montreal, for example. It would be looking at the questions of the fundamental problems with employment, schools and the drop-out rate of our children out of high school.
It would be looking at the reasons why people now have to use food banks and why youth are sleeping in the streets. That is the kind of research it could be doing. It could be coming up with some creative answers in terms of the debt, deficit and the other balance on the scale; fair, proper, social policies that could answer the crying needs of the everyday people out there, not the people who have been designing these disastrous kinds of policies that are of no avail to either the Science and Research Council or Canada Council.
I asked for a six-month hoist to give the government the opportunity to consult which it did not do. Now the government has the nerve to come in here and say I misquoted certain facts and information in committee. It said it is going to save $6 million and then it is going to save $5 million-a little correction in the middle of the text. It is going to be done in five years-no, now it is going to be done in three years. Then the government praises the Science Council because it is going to do some very careful and creative work to make this merger a far less costly organization, administratively. It talked about $217 million and the potential for saving $35 million in its operation.
The Canada Council has no choice because the government has cut its grants. What do you expect it to do?
It has to chop, chop, chop. It does not know where the budget is coming from or what the extent of the budget really is. It only knows this government is not committed to the well-being of the scientists and the research that needs to be done. It is not committed to supporting the arts and artists. It would be best if this section were totally removed-that would be the real world. That is what I expected the government would do if it had put this aside for six months and consulted, which it did not do.

Stubborn as the government is, it continues on the road to ruin. I believe it is a mistake, a serious mistake. The comments and options put forward by the member for Regina are very sensible. I was hoping that the government would listen but unfortunately I do not believe that it did.

With respect to the sunset clause which was referred to, I asked for a sunset clause. I am delighted that my colleague, the member from Winnipeg, placed a sunset clause in for debate. If the minister feels his sunset clause at six years is better than our sunset clause at five years, I will leave it to discussion around this table on the floor when we get to my colleague's Motion No. 40. Then we will look at which is the better option; six and five, yes or no. It is a matter of at least going back with a sunset clause because this is a ridiculous motion in the first place.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to speak on behalf of the amendments put forward by my colleague, the member for St. Boniface.
I think it should be stressed here this morning that I think the government is in error by not going along with the suggestions that are being made. What we want here is the best result possible. There are some things that have more or less fallen between the stools as far as this legislation is concerned that could be corrected.
As I said earlier, I am opposed to the doing away of the Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation. However, leaving that argument aside, I want to see some areas that are strengthened here.
April 20, 1993

One thing that bothers me and has obviously bothered the member for St. Boniface is that the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council is going to be losing its designation. That is why he made Motion No. 24. He is suggesting that the name of the organization to be created not just be the Canada Council but be known as the Arts and Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada. It is important to have this designation so we can indicate to people that we have an organization whose activities are reflected in the name. To do otherwise really gives short shrift to the arts and social sciences and to the humanities. I think this can be corrected by changing the name as suggested by the member for St. Boniface in Motion No. 24.
I also think it is important to look at the composition of the board of directors. The board of directors, according to this legislation, really does not have to have its membership from any particular designation of the sphere of influence that this board is to oversee. All the members could be from one area as opposed to another area. There could be those from the arts but not enough from the social sciences or the humanities. I think there should be something in this bill that designates that all of the spheres of influence of this new board are to be represented properly by adequate representation on the board of directors. These people should not be political patronage appointments by the government. They should be people with the proper, requisite knowledge to do the job that is required to be done.
I think we have a tremendous record in this country in the area that is going to be taken on by this new board. The fact that they have a tremendous history to live up to is going to require them to have the proper representation.
It is also important that the areas involved be reflected. In these various areas of the arts, social sciences and humanities, the only way we can show appreciation and convince the Canadian people that each area is getting the proper attention is by giving each the proper representation on the board of directors.
It has been very short-sighted of the government to say that the funding for this board will be reflected in one vote. I think that is wrong. I think what we are doing is really cutting the legs out from underneath this board
Government Orders
by doing that. I think the government, upon reflection, would have to agree to this. For the sake of a minor change, frankly, we can have the proper accountability, the proper reflection of the activities of this board by saying that instead of the one vote there would be three votes. There would be a vote for the social sciences, a second vote for the arts and a third vote for administration. I think it is in the interest of all members of the House, certainly in all the areas and spheres of influence reflected by this new organization, that the actual allotting of financing be reflected properly. I ask the government to consider that very carefully.
I think the member for St. Boniface has made an excellent point by saying that we really should not include in this new board the academic relations section of external affairs. This is to me totally incomprehensible. Why would we be bringing this group into this new organization? I do not understand it. Certainly there is no cost saving involved. In fact, there may be additional expenditures as a result. We are talking about Canadian students studying abroad. We are talking about foreign students studying in Canada.
With the present arrangement, when they are part of external affairs these students have the whole department as a support system. They have External Affairs representation in various countries, embassies, consulates and so on. They also have the proper representation that can link very well with this particular section. To say that foreign students will be now in a separate body apart from the rest of external affairs is counterproductive. I think this should be changed and I would ask the government to reconsider this and leave the academic relations section with external affairs.
I also want to mention Motion No. 40 with respect to the review. The previous speaker already mentioned that. I think the government's acknowledgement that a review is necessary is correct. I think the proposal in the suggested amendment by the member for St. Boniface is much superior to what the government is suggesting. The reason I say this is that Motion No. 40 put forward by the member for St. Boniface gives the provision teeth. It says that the review is to be conducted every five years, but the review is to be conducted by Parliament and the study goes back to Parliament for decision making.

April 20, 1993
Government Orders
I think that is vital because it involves Parliament in the whole process. I think that is certainly what the component parts of the new organization would want. I think that is what Canadians want.
We are talking about an organization that is part of the fibre of our country. I think that if we are going to make these changes then we should make the changes as meaningful as possible. We should reflect the component parts as much as possible and we should allow Parliament to have the input that it needs. Do not forget for a moment of course that Parliament represents every part of this country. We want to make sure that every part of this country has its views and its aspirations reflected in this new organization. Therefore, I think the review by Parliament is very important.
This is too important an area to let go and just to pass over. I want to ask the government to give very strong consideration to those amendments made by the member for St. Boniface because I think they will greatly strengthen what is intended.

Mr. Speaker, the essence of democracy is that a government governs with the consent of the governed.
We have just had a dissertation by the member for Terrebonne which indicates that that is the least concern of this particular government at this time. None of the points that he put forward had anything to do with the
people who are involved with the Canada Council and the humanities, arts and social sciences areas and do not have any real impact on these decisions.
In other words there was no consultation of any kind as far as the governed were concerned. These are the people who are going to be affected most. In other words democracy is the least worry of this particular government at this particular time. Maybe it is because it is just going into an election and it does not expect to be here after the election.
The essence of democracy is the consent of the governed. There has been no consent of anybody who is involved in these particular changes.
The essence of the amendments that we are debating today concerns something that the Canada Council people, the university people and the academics asked this government to look at. It is for the whole of part III to be dropped in its entirety.
They used as part of their argument for the dropping of Part III the fact that within the information provided to the committee and to the arts group that there were no savings except for 10 members of the government who probably would not lose their jobs anyway and who would be moved some place else. There would be no actual savings in the operation of the two councils if they are merged into one.
In the process of looking at these changes, there is no efficiency being indicated at all and there was no consultation with any of the bodies affected.
It has come to the point where I do not know why the government party which calls itself the Progressive Conservative Party does not delete the "Progressive" from its name. That is because what they are actually doing here is going back to what they had before 1978. The decision to change the council into two councils is a regressive move.
Consequently, I never did understand what Progressive Conservative meant. I think probably we should say once more-as my colleague here from the Liberal Party suggests-that we should change the name to the Regressive Conservative Party because that is what the party seems to be doing in this particular operation.
April 20, 1993

There was no consultation. In fact there was probably exclusion. There was no discussion on the changes that were going to be made in this by Part III of this act.
We recognize that after eight years in power the government is a little hesitant about using consultation. It has given consultation a bad name. It pretends it is going to consult, calls people together, seems to listen and then goes its own way.
That is the kind of consultation it has been carrying on.
I suppose maybe we should not blame it for not having consultation in this instance. Nobody believes that any consultation this government has done in the last few years has been of any value to the people who are being governed by its changes.
I can give you specific examples of consultation which has not been to the benefit of the people who are being governed. We have had thousands of hours of consultation relative to agriculture. None of that was taken into consideration when the decisions were made in agriculture. The decisions were made by the bureaucrats and in some cases by the members opposite.
The same thing is happening right now in development. The minister of development is here at the moment. There are a lot of changes being made in development that have nothing to do with the people who are being governed, the people of Canada.
We should be following the recommendations that have been made by the people who are most affected and not disorganising the provision of grants or the process by which we support research, the arts and so on in Canada.
We should look at part III, eliminate it and do a very basic and thorough study of what is necessary to perhaps save more money than we are now. The essence of democracy is only democracy if it happens with the consent of the governed.
I want to spend a couple of moments putting before this House some of the feelings of the people who are most affected by part III of Bill C-93.
For instance, the Canadian Association of University Teachers says that no prior consultation with any of the
Government Orders
SSHRC's stakeholders was conducted and no convincing rationale has ever been offered for this measure.
It goes on to say:
All that is being offered to date is a promise that the merger would be conducted among equal partners in a wholly new agency so as to ensure that the federal support for research in the social sciences and humanities would remain independent.
That is only a promise which none of the people involved really believe. It did not work before 1978 when these two agencies were separate and it is unlikely to work well in the future.
A second group is the federation representing the social sciences. It said almost the same thing:
After having carefully studied the proposed legislation, we remain very concerned about the future of social sciences in this country.
Again, there was no consent from or consultation with those people who are being governed.
The Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada and the university teachers said:
Lumping the social sciences and humanities with the arts does not make much sense.
They show how ridiculous it is to be regressive and go back to before 1978 without having a plan that is going to work and without saving any money. They go on to provide several quite workable alternatives which should be used instead of putting part III through.
This is an attack on the very essence of democracy. By going through with part III of Bill C-93, the government is not allowing the people who are most affected to have a say in the legislation which is going to be passed in this House.

Mr. Speaker, it is both tax time and budget time again. I want to call the attention of the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Revenue to an area of injustice in the tax system.
One of my constituents writes:
April 20, 1993

Many women (and some men) across this country, who are custodial parents following marital breakdown, are required by law to report receipt of child support payments as income and then pay taxes on this money.
In my opinion child support payments are not income but rather reimbursements for expenses incurred in raising children.
She goes on to say:
I receive what I consider to be a fair amount of money as child support but in reviewing my income tax returns for the past two years that I have been a single parent, I realize, with horror, that over 40 per cent of what I receive has been lost to me through increased income tax and lost child tax credit.
Without having expressly addressed the question of deductibility of the support payments from the payers' income, I contend that taxing the custodial parent is a major cause of single parent poverty and contributes to the hunger and misery of thousands of children in a country that is relatively affluent.
With a view to the upcoming budget I ask the ministers involved to review this piece of oppressive tax legislation which so viciously discriminates against the custodial parent in a broken marriage situation.

Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to remind members of the House that April 18 to 24 is National Organ Donor Awareness Week.
Professional and voluntary organizations encourage families to discuss and make a decision about organ donation before a tragedy occurs, and urge health professionals to examine how they might participate in the organ donation process.
I invite Canadians everywhere to consider organ donation and to sign a donor card or the consent portion of their driver's licence if they have not already done so. Decisions should be discussed with family and friends so that in the event of death the potential donor's wishes will be followed.
By doing this we can all give, and encourage others to give, the most valuable gift of all, the gift of life.
I wish everyone involved with National Organ Donor Awareness Week a very successful event.

Mr. Speaker, time and time again we are reminded that the federal agencies and departments are not respecting the Official Languages Act. Twenty-four years after the adoption of this law minorities must still fight for their rights in provinces and in the federal government.

The minister knows there is far too much air service available in Canada and the current competitive nature of service means that neither airline can make a profit from their monopoly of Canadian airspace.
If we are going to have in effect a monopoly arrangement in Canadian airspace with all of the flight patterns between Canadian cities controlled in favour of Canadian Airlines and/or Air Canada then surely the minister has an obligation to ration service so the carriers do not destroy themselves in stupid competition.

Mr. Speaker, the recent tragic death of well-known South African activist Chris Hani has sparked a new round of violence that threatens to undermine the struggle of the people of South Africa to end apartheid.
The continued violence, which has resulted in further loss of human life, must not be allowed to escalate. The government of Mr. de Klerk must thwart the efforts of those who wish to sabotage the forces of democracy and he must take the responsibility of finding ways to rekindle the positive attitudes that seemed to characterize events just a few weeks ago.
TTie relatively peaceful environment on the occasion of Mr. Hani's funeral was a tribute to his calls for peace and his commitment to negotiate a change. The majority of South Africans want peace and full democracy, and a majority of South African people want to create a better South Africa for all.
We in Canada must do all we can to support both those in government and opposition.
It is right that existing sanctions be continued until irreversible steps to the democratization of South Africa are taken. We recognize that the challenges are great but the opportunities and rewards for peaceful reform in South Africa are greater.

Mr. Speaker, last Friday evening I attended a meeting of some 150 part-time fishermen organized by the South Shore Independent Fishermen's Association. These fishermen fear that DFO's stated intention with respect to the definition of professional fishermen will exclude them even though some of them have been fishing for over 40 years.
They recognize the need to reduce the groundfish harvesting capacity of the Scotia-Fundy region. What they do not understand, and with some reason it seems to me, is why they who harvest only 1 per cent of the
available resource have apparently been targeted for elimination.
Since they have not been the source of the problem why should their elimination be deemed to be the solution? DFO has not satisfactorily answered this question.
If the status or future of part-time fishermen is to be altered in any way there must be full and thorough consultation with those to be affected. To date that has not happened.

Mr. Speaker, South Africans continue to mourn the brutal murder of Chris Hani, a respected leader and official of the African National Congress and the South African Communist Party.
Mr. Hani was one of the most vigorous opponents of the racist system of apartheid, fighting it from exile for three decades.
More recently he placed his faith in a shared future for all South Africans and worked in favour of a negotiated settlement. His assassination is one more senseless and tragic loss of life in a country where a whole generation of black leaders has been lost to violence.
His murder sparked widespread violence and rioting among South Africans and the fallout could threaten the process of reform.
I urge the Canadian government to make a strong statement condemning the assassination of Chris Hani and all violence in South Africa, particularly the continued activities of the security forces against black South Africans and the rise in white extremist violence.
As well we should urge the Government of South Africa to accelerate the timetable for free and democratic elections in that country.
Finally, I join many Canadians in hoping that the events of the last few weeks will prove to be one of the last times that apartheid claims the lives of the courageous men and women fighting for its disappearance.
On behalf of my colleagues we extend our deep condolences to the family of a true hero, Chris Hani.
April 20, 1993

Mr. Speaker, everyone recognizes the important role women's groups and associations play in our society, that is everyone but the conservative government which has cut the Secretary of State women's program funding for several years now, under the guise of austerity measures.

When will the Conservative government respect the rights of half our population?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate all those who participated in National Citizenship Week.
Last week thousands of people took the oath of citizenship in ceremonies from St. John's to Victoria. Many were Canadians who participated in ceremonies that reaffirmed their Canadian citizenship. Most of these were young people bom in Canada, and for them reaffirmation of their citizenship expressed their commitment to Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Yom Hashoah representatives from Jewish communities around the world, along with many non-Jewish neighbours, marked the 50th anniversary of the Warsaw ghetto uprising. Their horrible memories of this unspeakable moment of history have marked their lives yet their presence bespeaks their final triumph over evil, of survival, and of the continuity of the Jewish people.
The Holocaust was a war of genocide against the Jews. Six million, among them one million children, were murdered by the Nazis or their accomplices for no reason other than the fact of who they were. The uprising exemplified the courage not to submit to Nazi victimization but to live with dignity and fight for life, not to be led like sheep silent to the slaughter.
Their tenacity of spirit was also a form of resistance. The memory of this bravery is scorched on our minds and in our hearts.
Today we must do more than remember. We must take up the challenge to affirm justice and humanity for all people, particularly now in Bosnia. We must assure that the perpetrators of war crimes are brought to justice. Our own progress appears to have faltered. We must redouble our efforts to eliminate the scourge of racism and anti-Semitism from our world.
In so doing the fight to the death for human dignity of the ghetto fighters will not have been in vain.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to pay tribute to Yukon First Nations, successive Yukon territorial governments and all Yukoners who for the past 20 years have worked toward one goal, the passing of the Yukon land claim and self-government legislation.
This is no ordinary achievement. At a time when the world is full of conflict and strife the recent passing of these agreements in the Yukon legislature shows us what

April 20, 1993
Oral Questions
can be done in the name of justice, equality and a better future for all people.
These agreements are the foundation of a new era of co-operation and goodwill, a new era that rejects the inequities of a painful past and a troubled present and holds out hope for a future based on respect.
This is indeed a great achievement that will be celebrated and supported by each member of this House. I therefore call upon this government to introduce this historic legislation in the House of Commons and to ensure its quick passage.

having been long and loyal customers, now in their moment of greatest need they find they cannot get the time of day from their banks.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was going to compliment the Leader of the Opposition on his 30 years in Parliament yesterday and tell him that he apparently does not get more elegant as he gets older in his job.

%

April 20, 1993

My hon. friend refers to the IMF report which indeed quite properly points to all industrialized governments in regard to making certain that debt is reduced, that deficits to the extent humanly possible are eliminated, that privatizations occur, that interest rates are kept low, and that inflation and productivity are dealt with as well. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance; Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak on third reading on Bill C-102, which contains the legislative amendments to implement a number of excise tax and tariff measures announced over the past 20 months. Many of these proposals have already been implemented through notices of ways and means motions tabled at the time of their announcement. Among the measures are tariff changes to reduce cross-border shopping and a range of initiatives to address the problem of tobacco smuggling and tax evasion.
Hon. members are no doubt aware that the growth in tobacco smuggling over the past few years has had a profound economic and social impact. Domestic sales of tobacco products have fallen significantly over the last year and a half, particularly in some parts of the country. The result of falling tobacco sales has been a substantial loss in business for those in the wholesale and retail trade.
Criminal organizations are becoming increasingly involved in the packaging of tobacco products and are using the profits from illegal sales of tobacco to finance other criminal activities.
Tobacco smuggling and tax evasion have also had a serious impact on the fiscal and social policies of the federal government. Revenues from tobacco taxes have declined as Canadian smokers switched to contraband tobacco products. This decline in tobacco tax revenues, which are used to fund important government programs
Government Orders
and services, has considerably outpaced the decline in overall tobacco consumption. As well, government health policies to discourage smoking are being undermined by the availability of inexpensive tobacco on the black market.
Without strong action by the government, the level of smuggling would continue to increase, with the resulting costs for the public and private sectors alike. This concern was the basis for the enforcement and control measures announced by the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Revenue last spring to deter tobacco smuggling. Bill C-102 provides the legislative authority to implement these measures, which can be summarized as follows: tighter controls on the distribution and sale of duty-free tobacco products in Canada; improved markings on tobacco products to better identify duty-free tobacco products; the addition of "proceeds of crime" provisions to the Excise Act and the Customs Act to enable law enforcement agencies to seize the profits made by organized crime from tobacco smuggling and tax evasion; and significantly higher criminal penalties for people caught smuggling tobacco into Canada or selling contraband tobacco products in Canada.
On this last point, I would like to note that amendments were proposed during consideration of this bill by the legislative committee to further increase the penalties for the smuggling and illegal sale of tobacco products under the Excise Act and Customs Act. I am pleased to report that these amendments were approved by the committee and are included in Bill C-102 for consideration by hon. members today.
I should add that over the past year the government has allocated substantial new resources to Revenue Canada and the RCMP to enable these agencies to strengthen their enforcement efforts both at the border and within Canada. These additional resources, together with the higher penalties, new controls on the sale and distribution of duty-free tobacco and the addition of "proceeds of crime" provisions in this bill are vital components of the government's measures to address the tobacco smuggling problem and will improve the government's enforcement efforts in this area considerably.
This bill also implements the excise tax on tobacco products for export or for sale through duty-free shops that was announced in February 1992.

April 20, 1993
Government Orders
The purpose of this tax was to reduce the incentive to smuggle by narrowing the price differential between Canadian tobacco products for sale in the Canadian tax-paid market and those sold in other countries.
While the tax was effective in reducing the supply of contraband tobacco products in Canada in the weeks following its introduction, it quickly became apparent that its effectiveness would be severely limited in the longer term once suppliers in the U.S. were able to obtain Canadian-type tobacco products outside of Canada. The government therefore suspended collection of the tax in April 1992, when it announced the introduction of additional tobacco enforcement and control measures, which are among those I described a few moments ago.
Bill C-102 also addresses another difficulty Canadian wholesalers and retailers have had to face: cross-border shopping.
Last year the Minister of Finance indicated to the Canadian Retail Council's National Task Force on Cross-Border Shopping that, to help deal with this serious problem, the government would be prepared to remove tariffs on imported consumer products that are not made in Canada and are purchased by cross-border shoppers, where the tariff contributes to higher prices in Canada.
The task force identified a number of products and after consultations with all interested parties it was determined that the tariffs on about 25 products could be removed. These tariff removals represent approximately $1 billion worth of annual imports and about $60 million in duty. Examples are video cassette recorders, microwave ovens, sewing machines, cameras and telephone answering machines.
Canadian consumers benefit as lower prices for these imported goods are passed on by the retailers and wholesalers. The retailers and wholesalers, and the economy in general, benefit as these measures encourage consumers to shop in Canada.
The response to this initiative has been very positive. Department of Finance officials are continuing to work
with Canadian industry and the Retail Council of Canada to identify other consumer products on which tariffs can be removed.
I would also like to touch very briefly on some of the other excise and tariff measures contained in this bill.
Hon. members will recall that in the 1992 budget the Minister of Finance announced the elimination of the 8.5 cent per litre excise tax on the ethanol and methanol portions of blended fuels. This measure, which will be enacted by Bill C-102, will encourage the development and use of ethanol and methanol fuels made from renewable feedstocks. The use of these fuels provides a number of environmental benefits, such as a reduction in carbon dioxide emissions.
The bill also contains a number of other tariff changes. Most of these are technical but some of them remove duties in response to requests from Canadian businesses. These amendments cover a variety of products such as peach trays and light bars for emergency vehicles but in my view the most significant change is the extension of duty-free entry to materials and parts imported by manufacturers who make goods that are incorporated into other products that are exported.
Previously those manufacturers could only get a refund of duties after the finished products were exported. Immediate duty relief was restricted to manufacturers who were both importers of the parts and materials and exporters of the finished goods. The extension of this privilege to intermediate producers is a big step in improving the competitive position of those producers.
In conclusion, I would like to emphasize the importance of the provisions in Bill C-102. In particular, this bill contains important measures to address the crossborder shopping problem. As well, the measures that will be enacted by this bill to combat tobacco smuggling will ensure that Canadian enforcement agencies have the proper means to go after and dismantle the criminal organizations involved in the illegal tobacco trade.
I therefore ask hon. members to support the passage of this bill on third reading.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak today on Bill C-102.
April 20, 1993

Basically this bill responds to the cross-border shopping problem and provides additional measures to counteract tobacco smuggling. I think everyone here recognizes the problems of cross-border shopping and tobacco smuggling. We as legislators have been asked by the Canadian people to do something about this problem. I know that we all feel that not enough is being done to attack this epidemic and not enough is being done to attack the whole problem of contraband cigarettes.
This bill was introduced in consultation with the tobacco industry. It is aware of the seriousness of the problem of cross-border shopping and smuggling and understands that it has a role to play in doing something about this problem. However, while this bill takes a first step to deal with the problem of smuggled tobacco by changing packaging rules and imposing stricter penalties for those who deal in these products it does nothing to address the root of the problem, which is high tobacco taxes.
Today as we study this bill I would like to speak specifically about the major problem of smuggling tobacco products in this country because it greatly affects my area of Haldimand-Norfolk. My argument is this: I believe that excessively high taxation on tobacco has created a prohibition-like environment in which otherwise law-abiding citizens are either selling or buying smuggled tobacco.
People from every walk of life, young and old, professional and welfare recipients, are in on the illegal action. All feel that they are over-taxed and for this reason have convinced themselves that buying or selling illegal tobacco is socially acceptable. They think that taxes on cigarettes are too high and that it is not a crime to buy or sell them. Many ordinary Canadians feel no compunction about buying or bypassing this tax-related law. Canadians now wink at cigarette smugglers the same way as Americans winked at the American bootleggers of the 1920s.
Smuggling is dividing communities. It is dividing native communities, inspiring the creation of criminal conspiracies, increasing violence for retailers, and goes hand in hand with the drug trade. In fact, organized crime is turning its attention to the illicit trade of tobacco
Government Orders
because the profit from illegal tobacco is much greater than that of drugs and the penalties are not as severe.
There is no dispute in this country over the root cause of smuggling. It is high tobacco taxes which have become such a large component of the product's cost and price that they may offer a massive potential profit margin to those who are able and willing to acquire and trade in cigarettes on which no tax has been paid.
It is difficult to understand why a government would allow something illegal to occur right under its nose because it is politically correct to do so. In other words, because of pressure from non-smoking groups and my friend here in the NDP both federal and provincial governments are afraid to deal with the tobacco taxation problem. They would rather continue with their high taxation policy, which we all know is only conducive to smuggling.
One would think that the federal government, knowing that it has contributed to a billion dollar organized crime industry, might start taking seriously this whole problem of the sale of illegal tobacco. What I find so frustrating about this whole situation is that the solution is simple. We should roll back the taxes. This answer was not arrived at in recent days or recent weeks. The tobacco industry and many Canadians have been offering this government a clear solution. The rolling back of tobacco taxes is not only a peaceful solution to the problem but one which makes sheer common sense.
The fact of the matter is that the RCMP can no longer deal with the problem because the problem is just too big. The RCMP concedes that enforcement is not effective in curbing smuggling. It says what is even more problematic is that enforcement efforts will just drive the illicit tobacco trade underground and into the hands of organized crime, which I think for all of us is really a frightening thought.
After all, Canada has taken a lot of pride in the fact that it has been regarded as the number one country in the world in which to live. According to the UN, one of the reasons why it achieves such high marks is that it offers relative safety to Canadians. The nurturing of organized crime in Canada will not keep us at number one for very long.

April 20, 1993
Government Orders
To conclude, I would like to offer some facts about the industry and about tobacco fanners and how tobacco taxation has come to the attention of this House. I believe that they all should be very carefully considered.
The contraband tobacco trade has a street value of over $1 billion. The tobacco black market is costing federal and provincial governments an estimated $1.4 billion a year in lost tax revenue robbing Ontario's 1,200 tobacco growers of nearly $20 million in lost markets. It really jeopardizes 60,000 Canadian jobs.
Smokers pay up to $47.13 for a legal carton of 200 cigarettes of which the manufacturer gets $7.79. Distributors and retailers get $3.38 and the remaining $35.96 goes to federal and provincial coffers.
Illegal cigarettes can be had for as little as $22.50 a carton. A single pack which sells for as much as $6.50 legally can be bought for almost half at $3.50.
High taxes are not turning people off cigarettes. They are simply sending them underground. These high taxes are only costing governments.
The tobacco industry supports directly or indirectly the jobs of some 60,000 Canadians in growing, manufacturing, distribution and in the retail sectors.
The large increases imposed by the federal and provincial governments in the 1980s were primarily responsible for the loss of some $5,000 tobacco-related jobs and the closure of four manufacturing plants.
Most of those jobs were in my area of Haldimand- Norfolk. Over the last 10 years, cigarette taxes have increased some 620 per cent. Let me repeat that. In the last 10 years, cigarette tax increases have come to around 620 per cent.
This figure compares to an alcohol tax increase of just 68 per cent, a personal income tax increase of 66 per cent and a corporate tax increase of very little.
The RCMP believes that higher Canadian taxation has meant bigger and better organized crime groups getting involved. Enforcement is never succeeded. It seems that the tighter the regulations become, the more organized and sophisticated the smugglers become. The RCMP describes the situation as "out of control".
The rural economy of an entire area is at stake and it is not just the farmers. Many small businesses depend on the viability of the tobacco industry especially in my area.
It is obvious that tobacco products will continue to be used in Canada.
The government must now face whether it wishes to export Canadian jobs through the tobacco industry and through a misguided taxation policy that disadvantages Canadians and allows American farmers and manufacturers to take over legitimate economic activity.
It is shameful that the government has fostered a tax policy which will devastate our domestic tobacco industry while pushing the economic benefits of producing this legal product across the border.
Of greater consequence, governments continue this taxation policy that has created a sophisticated smuggling network that the RCMP admits it cannot curtail. Surely, we as legislators must re-evaluate our taxation policy on tobacco. It is time we rolled back these taxes.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on Bill C-102. That previous speech by the Liberal member was shocking. I kept asking him whether he was actually speaking on behalf of the Liberal Party and whether this was their total policy.
April 20, 1993
I always speak on behalf of the Liberals.

That is nice to know. This is the official stand of the Liberal Party. They support the tobacco industry in Canada and oppose health measures that have significantly reduced the use of cigarettes in this country and the incidence of death from tobacco.
It is not like the NDP that goes with marijuana.
We have to start to talk about what the consequences are in this country of the use of tobacco products.
Why not just talk about the bill?

What is obviously known is that 55,000 Canadians die every year because of illness related to tobacco use. If the Liberals think that is funny then one should talk to 55,000 families that have lost then-husbands, wives, sons and daughters because of tobacco consumption.
This is one of the most serious health problems facing the industrial world and is being pushed and pushed by tobacco companies into the developing world. Sales are being aimed at children in Canada and sales are being aimed at children in the Third World countries.
Over the last number of years, the federal government, in conjunction with the provincial governments, has initiated a national campaign to reduce the consumption of tobacco. It is one of the better things that this government has done. It has done it based on two or three kinds of policies.
First of all it did it by increasing the taxes on cigarettes. Every time there has been a dramatic increase of 25 cents to 50 cents on a package of cigarettes, 100,000 Canadians quit smoking. It was done by an educational program that has educated people about the dangers of smoking. It did it by bringing in programs that insisted that cigarette products contain health warnings.
This bill that was brought in some time ago also contained an ability to put an export tax on tobacco products. What we have learned in this country is that most cigarettes that are exported are illegally smuggled back into the country.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: It is 90 per cent.

It is 90 per cent and even more. Last year the government put an $8 export tax on a carton of cigarettes and took the profit away from smuggling.
Government Orders
There was no profit to be made in bringing those cigarettes back into Canada because one had already paid one's taxes on them. One could not bring them back in tax free.
In March 1992 there was an export of 164 million cigarettes. Then the government was lobbied by people like Vista. The Liberals wanted to make sure that one could increase the sale of cigarettes. There was lobbying by the tobacco industry and the manufacturers' association. This included such lobbyists as Bill Neville who is the Prime Minister's former chief of staff. There were threats. The tobacco industry said it would stop buying tobacco in Canada and would close all of the manufacturing plants in Canada. The federal government capitulated and withdrew the tax.
Here is what happened as soon as it withdrew the tax. The export and therefore the illegal smuggling of cigarettes back into Canada jumped dramatically. In March 1992 there were 164 million cigarettes exported. In May 1992 after the government capitulated and withdrew the export tax, that figure jumped to 958 million cigarettes, which is an increase of 650 per cent.
We all know that these are exported and then smuggled back into Canada. All the government did was to make it profitable again to have cigarettes smuggled back into this country.
In March 1992 there were 39 million kilograms of fine cut tobacco exported because there was the export tax making it unprofitable to smuggle these cigarettes back into Canada. In May 1992 after the government had capitulated and given in to the hardball tactics of the tobacco industry, the exports jumped from 39 million to 366 million kilograms of fine cut tobacco. That is an increase of 938 per cent.
The government said: "We will now again make it profitable for the smugglers". It had an impact. The federal government lost $800 million in tax revenue that it could have collected and the provinces probably lost a similar amount.
When the government was playing around with putting in the export tax the industry must have had tremendous anticipation. They somehow knew what was going to happen. When the government announced that it was going to put in an export tax, one company knew in advance somehow to ship out of Canada 50 truckloads of cigarettes before the tax was implemented.

April 20, 1993
Government Orders
We do need a level playing field. The Liberal solution is obviously to make our taxes lower on cigarettes and comparable with that of the United States.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Who said that?

That is what your colleague says. That is what he is advocating. Cut the tobacco tax.
Of course we know that if we reduce the price of cigarettes then the consumption of cigarettes will simply go up.
In Canada we have developed probably the most effective program to combat tobacco consumption of any country: education, high taxes and warning labels on cigarettes.
The tobacco industry said it would co-operate with the government if the government dropped the export tax on cigarettes. I want to just point out what has been done for that co-operation. Immediately afterward there was a code to be put on cigarettes so that if they were smuggled back into Canada we could trace where they came from.
However the tobacco companies knew that they did not want to be traced. They might have been exporting cigarettes to a particular wholesaler and then these were being smuggled back into Canada.
All the tobacco companies got together and now export all their cigarettes to one warehouse in Syracuse, New York. If cigarettes are smuggled back into Canada they can only be traced to that warehouse in Syracuse, New York.
Because it is outside Canadian jurisdiction, we have no ability to control it or insist on information. That is the type of co-operation the tobacco industry has given us to reduce the problem of cigarette exports.
For the last two or three years the industry has fought dramatically through the courts to try to stop the proper labelling of cigarettes with health warnings. It has tried to ensure that the labelling required on cigarettes and inserts that warns about the health problems of cigarette consumption is not effective. The industry does not want to have nice, bold colours. They are too contrasting and
easily readable. The industry has held it up in the courts for the last couple of years and has lost.
The government is now in the process of bringing forward new regulations which are going to make the labelling more stringent.
I want to talk about an issue that has been raised about farmers. We in this party have repeatedly said that instead of helping farmers grow a product that kills people worldwide, the government has a responsibility to assist tobacco farmers change to other types of crops. That is a solution. We cannot continue to support an industry that kills 55,000 Canadians a year. We cannot abandon the farmer and take away his livelihood. We must develop adjustment programs to help that farmer move to other productive crops.
In Canada, when we look at who is calling on the government to do certain things and whose side they are on, we very quickly realize that the people who are working in the best interest of Canadians are calling for the government to find its courage again and put an export tax on tobacco. These are people in organizations like the Canadian Medical Association, the Canadian Cancer Society and the Heart and Stroke Foundation. Every medical group across this country says tobacco kills 55,000 Canadians a year. That is half a million Canadians between now and the turn of the century.
People are standing up and advocating that the government should not continue with its program that has been effective. It should roll back taxes so cigarettes become cheaper which would increase consumption. Remember, every time the price of cigarettes is increased from 25 cents to 50 cents a package, 100,000 Canadians stop smoking.
There is another reason why my party and I side with people in organizations like the Canadian Medical Association. It is because the cost to taxpayers in terms of health care is horrendous. It is estimated that 10 per cent of all our acute care hospital beds are taken up with people who have smoking-related illnesses. If we could suddenly save a minimum of 10 per cent of our acute care dollars in this country we would be able to do something far more effective. We would have lots of money available for adjustment programs to help farmers move into other kinds of crops.
April 20, 1993

I want to finish by talking about the morality of the tobacco industry. Confidential documents were brought forward over the last couple of years which show that the tobacco industry deliberately aims its programs and advertising at minor children. It knows that 80 per cent or more of people who start smoking start before they are 18. If they have reached the age of 18 and are not smokers they are not going to be smokers. In spite of its denial, the tobacco industry has done life-style advertising and promotions aimed at getting younger and younger people to smoke.
In the Third World countries where there is no legislation to control the advertising of tobacco, the industry is even more blatant. It openly aims its products at 12 and 13 year-olds. It hands out free cigarettes to minors in Asian countries, Pacific rim countries and Thailand to promote them because its share of the market in North America has gone down.
Why are the tobacco companies so frightened about what is happening in Canada? They see that other countries are starting to look at our success in reducing the consumption of tobacco. They see it is a threepronged success based on increasing taxation, continuing a level of export tax to make it unprofitable to smuggle cigarettes back into Canada, education about the dangers of cigarettes and labelling.
I hope this bill will go through without coming back to this House to reimpose the export tax on cigarette products. Is this government on the side of the big tobacco producers or on the side of the 55,000 Canadian families who lose their loved ones each year. Which side will we be on?
The government and the Liberals must have the courage to stand up and be on the side of Canadians. We must say we will reduce tobacco consumption and be on the side of those 55,000 Canadians who will lose their husbands and wives each year. We must reimplement the export tax.

Mr. Speaker, I want to let the hon. member know that the Liberal Party of Canada is firmly behind the Canadian farmer and will continue to support the Canadian farmer.

He suggested in his speech that he knew how to solve the problems of tobacco farmers, which is clearly NDP gibberish. He has probably never been to see a tobacco farm. He is probably not aware that the government came out a year ago with a $32 million program to help the Canadian tobacco farmer. Do you know how much of that money has gone to the tobacco farmer? None. Absolutely zero. The government announced with great fanfare that it was going to help them diversify into other programs and then cancelled the AEI program to help them get into other areas.
Canadian tobacco farmers, knowing the future of the industry, have gone to the government to ask it to be involved in NISA. The hon. member may not know what NISA is, but NISA would give these farmers an opportunity to be like the com and grain farmers in our agricultural community. It would give them the opportunity to invest in their future and help them get through the highs and lows. But the government has not allowed them into this great program.
The hon. member speaks a lot about the Liberal Party supporting the tobacco fanners that he refers to as murderers. He knows I have not spoken in this House on behalf of the tobacco manufacturers. I have spoken on behalf of the Canadian tobacco farmers and our tobacco communities that depend on these farms.
Is the hon. member aware that every time he gets up and talks like that, sending out this misinformation to Canadians, it hurts Canadian farmers and specifically Canadian tobacco farmers in our communities and our small business people who depend on these farmers?

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate that question because I think it goes to the heart of the issue. This member is saying that if it is profitable and kills people it is just too bad for those 55,000 people. He is determined to continue this profitable business that kills people.
I am sorry but the member cannot have it both ways. Yes, as tobacco consumption goes down tobacco farmers are going to be hurt. I have no doubt about it. That is why my party and I have called upon the government to put in realistic programs to help tobacco farmers switch to other programs. We should not continue to provide programs to help them through the highs and lows and allow them to continue to produce a crop that we know is dangerous.

April 20, 1993
Government Orders
If we have to make a choice on this issue-and I guess being in government is all about making choices about whose side we are on-I think it is fairly clear. Research over the last 25 years has clearly and unequivocally shown that the use of tobacco products is dangerous to a person's health and in fact causes death to 55,000 people a year.
Somebody said there are 5,000 tobacco farmers in Canada. Is that 10 deaths per tobacco farmer?
We have to ask ourselves what position we should be supporting. Should we support the continued escalation of the use of tobacco knowing its cost to the health care system and to individuals in terms of their life expectancies and health, or do we take steps to systematically reduce tobacco consumption?
I applaud this government because it has consistently, until it backed off on the export tax, had an integrated policy to allow for a gradual reduction in tobacco through education.

Mr. Speaker, we heard a spirited defence just a little while ago of the merits of the tobacco industry and the consumption of tobacco. I wonder if the health critic for the Liberal Party agrees with the position of the spokesman for the Liberal Party on the consumption of tobacco.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The question has to be directed to the hon. member for Surrey North.
Is he going to answer the question, as the former health minister?

Mr. Speaker, how he describes the tobacco industry is accurate. Experience, and bitter experience, teaches us that. On the one hand, it says it does not want young people to smoke but on the other hand it promotes smoking for young people.
I think we can say that Canada today is a leader in the anti-smoking crusade. We have had difficulty, for example, with tobacco farmers. I disagree with the hon. member that it is easy for tobacco farmers to switch over to other crops that are at least as financially beneficial to them as is tobacco. The land in the Delhi area is possibly not as suited to replacement crops. That is a reality we face.
Having said that though, there is a bottom line. I believe the tobacco industry is an amazing industry. It is the only industry that promotes death, destruction, fire, health loss, illness and a shortened life span and makes it glamorous. It is the only industry that is able to do that. It has a phenomenal marketing ability.
If one listens to my words they sound very harsh but they are absolutely accurate. Take a look. What next step does the member feel that Canada should take to promote public health policy, and particularly the reduction of smoking, especially among young people in Canada?

Mr. Speaker, I welcome that question. I would also say that the member's words do not sound harsh at all, they sound honest.
We have advocated that the next step is probably to stop the tobacco companies from promoting cultural and particularly sports events and using their names in doing so. Australia has simply stopped them from promoting any kind of events that they use their name in.
The other thing is to continue and maybe even escalate the health education programs that the government has initiated to inform people about the dangers of tobacco, particularly to inform young people and counteract the idea that to smoke is glamorous, macho and makes young women very attractive. We have to be able to counter the kind of glamorous image the tobacco industry likes to portray.
I agree with the hon. member very much that it is the only industry in the world that glamorizes its product knowing that it creates death.

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Mazankowski that Bill C-102, an act to amend the Customs Tariff, the Excise Act, the Excise Tax Act, the Customs Act, the Criminal Code and a related act, be read the third time and passed.

Mr. Speaker, it is my privilege to speak on Bill C-102, which is a very complicated bill for a lot of different Canadians.
I have very mixed feelings about the bill and certainly I can understand what many other Canadians have said. There certainly is a health problem with regard to smoking. Everyone in this House and everyone in this country recognizes that to be a true fact.
We also know that smoking is very tax-high revenue for the government. As mentioned earlier by my colleague, taxes have gone up some 600 per cent in the last 10 years. This shows that maybe the wrong focus has gone toward smoking and I would say alcohol as well. We look at a government that is promoting through taxation smoking and alcohol, in fact deriving the greatest share of the revenues through both, and yet many in this country would say we question the value of cigarettes and alcohol.
Government Orders
My colleagues on the far left of the House, the New Democratic Party, have suggested that there are extreme health problems. From hearing my colleagues from the NDP and as well some of the colleagues from across the way I have to ask why the policy is not to ban smoking in this country. It seems to me that if the health problem they are presenting and they are saying they will end the smoking issue, then it would be a logical step to ban smoking in this country. I certainly do not think that has been done either by the government side or by the NDP, who purport to be the great saviours in terms of health problems.
Because they are hypocrites.

There is a major economical question involved with this bill. Absolutely no one will debate that $34 per carton of cigarettes is a very healthy revenue for the government. It has escalated so much in the last 10 years that it has become a law enforcement problem. That problem then starts to stem out into organized crime which is smuggling cigarettes into this country, causing a second social problem which is the illegal use of cigarettes in the country.
Many people in the RCMP as well as in customs and excise have compared it to our prohibition days with alcohol. Now many organized crime groups are bringing cigarettes in by the truckload and distributing them throughout the country. These illegal cigarettes are raising revenue in this country of as much as $1 billion annually. That is a tremendous problem for our law enforcement agencies. I would say that part of this bill does deal with that problem and corrects some of that. The imposition of fines of up to $200,000, the extra fines that would be imposed on people who bring illegal cigarettes into the country, is good. That portion of the bill is going to stop Canadian-made cigarettes from going over to the United States and then being brought back into Canada.
The real crux of the problem is the fact that we have escalated the cost of a product that many people in this country legally use, are addicted to and have chosen to use. We have escalated the cost of that product so much that people from every walk of life in Canada, from every sector of our society, are purchasing cigarettes illegally and at the most economical prices. It is a tendency that I see happening not only in the tobacco industry but in all facets of Canadian life.

April 20, 1993
Government Orders
In talking with people over the last few years I have found that they are very upset with tax increases. People are very upset with the high cost of living in this society, whether it is income taxes, taxes that have been imposed through goods and services or taxes that are coming through our excise areas.
We know that the tax record of increase, increase, increase has taken money from the Canadian consumers' pockets and increased their costs as much as 50 per cent, 60 per cent, or 70 per cent in the last eight years.
We know that this is a major problem for Canadians in tough times. Canadians are looking at the amount of money they are putting out in taxes and saying that it is far too much.
I am watching the Tory leadership campaign going on and I certainly understand from it that we have a problem. Everybody is saying: We can stop the extra spending in this country. We can stop the huge tax increases. We can slow down the debt and the deficit.
This is a situation that has developed dramatically over the last eight years. It is a problem that every Canadian speaks about in coffee shops. It is a problem they speak about in homes when they are sitting around the dinner table. It is a problem we as a nation have to face.
Is the government overtaxing to a point that is causing a lot of normal law-abiding citizens to purchase articles that should not be for sale? They should not be taxed as high as they are. I think it is causing another crime situation in this country.
With regard to the health issues, the crime issue, the excessive cost of cigarettes and the tax issue, we have very mixed up, in terms of its concerns, legislation coming forward that does not seem to be consistent.
If I take what my colleague across the way said about the fact that cigarettes must be stopped or what the member from the NDP said, I would assume they are going to step forward to ban cigarettes in this country. Then we will have a real undercurrent of growth because people do choose to smoke in this country.
It is our responsibility to make sure that the interests of all Canadians are treated fairly. I do not believe that high taxation on cigarettes, the way it has been, and the laws that we are coming down with are resolving the core problem. The core problem here is another matter of taxation and enforcement.
I support stopping the illegal entry of cigarettes into the country and punishing those who do it. That is a good measure. However, we have missed the core point in this issue which is overtaxation.

Mr. Speaker, after listening to the various speeches about the tobacco industry and the rest, I must say this is something we could talk about for a long time. People want to put a stop to youth directed advertising by cigarette manufacturers. They want to restrict cigarette smoking generally, but after all, people are free to choose and if they want to smoke, there is not much we can do about it.
There is another aspect we should consider. Recently, the tobacco industry has become a criminal element in our society. How did it get this way? In the past few years there was an incredible increase in excise taxes on tobacco and cigarettes and now taxes are so high that people have started to smuggle. In other words, excessive taxes have created a smuggling industry.
The hon. member from Toronto told me that last year the federal government lost more than $750 million.
Taxes have created a smuggling industry and the only logical way to deal with the problem is to cut taxes, if only for a year or two, in order to stabilize the situation. Then we can see how we can stop the smuggling and prevent this industry to engage in criminal activities.
Representatives from my riding, including Mr. Denis Savard, came here to discuss the problem. Mr. Savard showed a lot of common sense in what he said.
We would have to reduce taxes on cigarettes, if only temporarily, to deter smuggling and prevent the cigarette industry to engage in criminal activities. That is the real problem. We have to deal with this problem first and then we can find ways to stop smuggling altogether.
April 20, 1993

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this debate today on Bill C-102.1 want to speak very briefly on the issue of taxes and tobacco smuggling.
I want to put on record first of all that I too am very concerned about the volumes of tobacco being smuggled. About one pack in six that is consumed in Canada is indeed smuggled. It represents about $1.6 billion in federal and provincial tax revenues. Smuggling profits are estimated to be about $800 million. This represents 48 million cartons of cigarettes, eight times that of 1990, an increase of 650 per cent in smuggling in two years.
This is primarily because governments kept insisting they were going to raise the taxes on cigarettes and tobacco at both federal and provincial levels. Of course in doing so, on the pretext that it is a health risk, and we admit that it is, they have created a whole new underground economy in smuggling. That underground economy applies not just to tobacco but also applies to alcoholic beverages.
The tax rate in Canada for example is 67 per cent, compared to the United States which is 30 per cent. In Europe it is 75 per cent. The difference between the price of a carton of Canadian cigarettes in Canada versus the United States is about $35 per carton. It is not much wonder that there has been a vast increase in the volume of smuggling.
These tax increases have indeed created an underground economy, just as the GST is contributing to an underground economy based on cash being paid for services. That in itself is becoming a very serious problem in this country. We warned the government during the GST debate that this would happen, but of course it turned a blind eye.
The legislation as originally drafted would have unfairly penalized Canada's land frontier duty free shop industry in an attempt by the government to correct problems created by the government's regressive tax regime and lax enforcements. The original clause 73 would have regulated the sales of duty free shops. In terms of correspondence, one operator who lives close to my riding said: "Presently all Canadian duty free shop operators are adhering to a one carton, two tin limit on all sales of cigarettes and fine cut tobacco".
Government Orders
The reason for this is that these duty free shop operators recognized the problem and did not want to be part of it. They voluntarily, as an organization of then-own people, put on a limit of what they would sell to people moving out of Canada, whether it is tourists from the United States or Canadians going to the United States.
The question then is why proceed with legislation limiting the sales from Canadian duty free shops if it has been demonstrated and recognized by the Department of Finance that the Canadian duty free shops are not part of the smuggling problem. At a time when the Canadian duty free shop industry as a whole is facing significantly increased competition from the United States, the only consequence of such a restrictive action would be to provide United States retailers with an additional competitive advantage and the subsequent loss of millions of dollars in tourist revenues.
The Canadian duty-free shop industry plays a key role in the Canadian economy through its employment of hundreds of Canadian workers and the generation of substantial tax and revenue dollars for the federal and provincial governments. The vast majority of the duty free shop industry is composed of small to medium sized businesses owned by Canadian citizens.
I had the privilege of being on the steering committee as a co-chair of that original committee that set up the Canadian duty free shop criteria. I am very proud of what these people have done. I am proud of the leadership they have shown in this regard and certainly I am very pleased that they voluntarily took the lead to try to control this terrible problem.
There has been an amendment passed in committee that recognizes their concerns and clause 73 no longer includes these duty free shops. Of course that means recognition of the fact that they are not part of the smuggling problem.
Over the last 10 years federal tobacco taxes have increased by 18.7 per cent per year on average and provincially 18.1 per cent. In 1980-81 the federal government collected $811 million in tobacco taxes. In 1990-91 the federal government collected $2.25 billion in taxes from tobacco. It has increased the taxes by 47 per cent since 1988 alone. Total tobacco sales by producers in 1991 totalled $310 million of which the federal government collected $2.25 billion in taxes. The entire Department

April 20, 1993
Government Orders
of Agriculture budget could be paid for on the tax collected on tobacco alone in this country.
A producer producing 90,000 pounds of tobacco will earn about $180,000. The federal government will collect $10 million in taxes on that particular producer's crop alone. It will yield well over $5 billion in taxes at the two levels of government in 1991-92 not including the GST.
Gradually the police and law enforcement people are in fact getting control of the situation. They are doing it slowly but surely. The LCBO, the Liquor Control Board of Ontario, estimates that one of every ten bottles of liquor consumed in Ontario is being either smuggled or bootlegged. The cigarette industry indicates that one in nine cigarettes obtained in Canada has been obtained illegally.
The Canadian Tobacco Manufacturers Council collected discarded cigarette packages after events last month and discovered that about 37 per cent of them had been smuggled. The LCBO estimated that Ontario residents spent more than $700 million for illegal liquor last year or about 13.5 per cent of the province's total liquor sales.
Meanwhile the revenues or the sale volume of LCBO has dropped by $60 million. This shows you the magnitude of the problem that has been brought about by the increased federal and provincial taxes. The RCMP said tobacco seizures have almost doubled in the last year. The force made about 3,000 seizures last year, which is up from 1,570 in 1991.
In a London Free Press article of March 20, 1993 the Quebec minister of revenue hinted that Ottawa and the provinces are considering lowering taxes on tobacco in a bid to curb the growing contraband cigarette trade. The Quebec revenue minister gave the figure that one in every three cigarettes sold in Quebec, Ontario and the west is contraband.
However although the Quebec minister may have seen the light, the federal government in Ottawa certainly has not. The article goes on to quote a senior official from the Department of Finance: "We are not at this point considering cutting taxes, certainly not actively".
The Tillsonburg Independent is a weekly newspaper in Tillsonburg, Ontario, which is the heart of tobacco country. The editorial of March 23, 1993 quotes the mayor of Tillsonburg's testimony before an Ontario legislative committee. He states that high taxation merely increases the already burgeoning share of the market that is in the hands of the smuggling industry.
We recognize the seriousness of the smuggling industry and we certainly hope that this will help relieve that problem. In terms of the health issue as spoken to by others earlier here today, I want to just point out the double standard we have here about the serious health issue as it concerns cigarettes.
I submit and I have submitted before in this House that the use of MMT in gasolines is an equal health risk. I call on the government to ban the use of this substance because there are alternatives available to MMT that are environmentally friendly and are not health risks. Surely if the government is serious about the use of tobacco and the risk to health, it has to be equally as serious about the use of MMT in gasoline where the victims are the young children of this nation.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to take a few minutes to comment on this afternoon's debate. First of all the bill before us today is many-sided. On the one hand, it will benefit the ethanol industry to some extent, and I am sure that I speak for all parliamentarians in this House when I say that it is about time we came up with such an initiative.
My colleague from Stormont-Dundas and myself have met with our local seaway group. They want to go about setting up an ethanol plant in our area.
