The hon. member for Lambton-Middlesex has been an advocate for the ethanol industry for a good long time in this House and I want to congratulate him as well.
I would now like to take a moment to address the cigarette smuggling issue.
April 20, 1993



Prior to the passage of the bill, prior to this bill being introduced, the fine for illegally importing cigarettes was nothing more than a joke. I complained in this House some two years ago about the effect of the absence of meaningful laws to curb smuggling.
As an example, under the present act a first offence right now for illegally importing cigarettes is a $50 fine. That must be very discouraging. That is about the profit on two cartons of cigarettes. For each subsequent offence the fine is $200.
Now we have fines not exceeding $10,000 and 12 months in jail. That is starting to make a bit of sense toward curbing the illegal importation of cigarettes in Canada. There has to be more done.
First I want to join with others who have said that there must be meaningful assistance for tobacco farmers in Canada to aid them in their transition to other crops and in recognizing all the difficulties that entails.

If you count three shifts a day, seven days a week, one needs five people in order to have one on duty at any one time. That means there are all of three people at the best of times when there are no holidays on duty to patrol that area where the smuggling is going on.
It would be a mistake to pretend that is a native-only problem. That is wrong. Gangs from Montreal and Toronto have virtually taken control of the smuggling in our area.
Finally, the union representing the customs and excise employees issued a statement last week condemning the government for cutbacks in customs employees when we should be increasing them in an effort to curb that contraband. That is what we need to do.
In terms of whether or not an export tax works, I am not sure. The bill contains that provision. I am not personally against it.
However, there is a problem and it might as well be stated. At the present time there is nothing that prevents Canadian tobacco manufacturers from establishing a

plant using the same product name and the same everything else in a package that looks virtually identical right across the border. It can then export those cigarettes to Canada in packages that look virtually the same as the ones that are shipped to the United States and that are smuggled back in at the present time.
Those are kinks and problems that the government will really have to work hard on. With that we have pretty well reached the hour of five o'clock. I will end my remarks for today and I will continue at the next sitting of the House.

speakeroldname: Mr. John R. Rodriguez (Nickel Belt) moved:
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, a National Securities Regulator
should be created to address the issue of overlapping federal and
provincial securities regulation.
He said: Mr. Speaker, my motion today calls on the government to consider the creation of the establishment of a national securities regulator.
The purpose and the reason given in my motion for establishing this is to address the issue of overlapping federal and provincial jurisdictions. Thirty years ago the royal commission on banking and finance recommended that the federal government take the lead in encouraging the development of "high and uniform standards of security legislation and regulation in Canada" by establishing a federal regulatory agency. That was 30 years ago.
Were you here 30 years ago?

I was not here 30 years ago. I could not be here and be as young looking as I am today. The arguments and the conclusion of that royal commission are as relevant today, probably even more so today than they were 30 years ago.
What has happened over the ensuing 30 years of course is the revolution in communication technology. There is the deregulation of financial institutions that has taken place. There is the internationalization of credit. There are all sorts of challenges and yet Canada among all the of the industrialized nations of the world is the only industrialized nation without a national securities regulator. The royal commission of the day had reasons to recommend that there be a national securities regulator. I also had reason to mention it in my motion. One reason was to eliminate much of the duplication and the lack of uniformity in regulations.
We have to understand the structure. The provinces are responsible for regulating security systems, so we have 10 provinces with 10 sets of regulations. Where the institution comes under federal jurisdiction there is a set of federal rules as well. There is a jungle of jurisdiction out there, often overlapping and often with no uniformity. It seems to me that having a national securities regulator would lead the provinces to establish a vety high set of federal standards. That should be uppermost in the minds of legislators.
If there were a national securities regulator it would increase the standard of regulation across the country in light of the ability of Canada to interface with other jurisdictions that have national standards of security regulations such as the United States, for example. The United States has the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. The U.S. commission has no counterpart in Canada with which it can interface. It has to interface with provincial regulators, and of course in each jurisdiction there is a different set of rules.
It is important to begin establishing a set of rules that we can project internationally. It would be setting the rules as large borrowers attempt to avoid the intermediation of banks and go to the international market for their funds. They often do that by selling securities directly. There must be a way to establish some sense of uniformity and some sense of standards.
I can give an example of a case where there was an overlapping of jurisdiction among the provinces. In this case it was between two provinces, the province of British Columbia and the province of Ontario. My colleague is from British Columbia. He will remember the Bennett-Doman case. It was a perfect example in which the former premier of British Columbia, Bill Bennett, and his brother Russell had been charged with insider trading in the stock of Doman Industries Limited. The defendants resided in B.C. but Doman's shares were traded exclusively on the Toronto Stock Exchange. The alleged illegal trading was effected through the Toronto Stock Exchange computer assisted trading system, a national communications system.
The B.C. government and the Ontario Securities Commission both laid charges against the Bennetts in early 1989. They were acquitted in the B.C. provincial court in May 1989. The Ontario Securities Commission dropped the charges in Ontario. The argument was that the legal principle of double jeopardy prohibited another trial on the same offence and set of facts.
The commission decided to proceed with a regulatory hearing into the case, but that case had to be abandoned the following year when the Supreme Court of Ontario ruled that the OSC could not compel the Bennetts to provide testimony. Justice Steele stated in his judgment that the court had no power "to assist the tribunal outside Ontario". It is a perfect example of where the national securities regulator could have brought the Bennetts to heel, if we had had a national securities commission with standardized rules. I thought I would use that one example to clearly illustrate the lack of
April 20, 1993

uniformity and of a sense of continuity across the country with respect to a national securities regulator.
We are almost there. We have global markets for securities, bonds and equities 24 hours a day. Interprovincial and international trade in securities are growing in importance. The key reasons are the growing importance of the securities markets and the allocation of credit. I mentioned that borrowers, large corporations, can now avoid the intermediation of banks and go directly to the markets by floating securities.
According to the Toronto Stock Exchange chairman Michael Edwards, cross-border equity trading surged from $73 billion U.S. in 1979 to $1.44 trillion U.S. in 1990. In these circumstances it is fairly obvious a system organized around provincial boundaries, a regulatory system based on provincial boundaries, is fairly well anachronistic and inadequate.
Right on.
I am starting to wonder about my position now. The hon. member for Mississauga South says: "Right on". That scares me because he is a friend of the trusts.
That is right, and you are a friend of the big banks.

He is the original trust buster.
There is increased pressure to improve and harmonize disclosure requirements to get rid of inconsistencies. Regulators need it to do a better job and investors want it because it facilitates their understanding and decision making. It would also result in a cut in the cost and paperwork involved in registering the same security in several provinces.
A second reason is that only a federal securities regulator would prevent competitive deregulation wars between provincial regulators. Competitive deregulation would harmonize trade in securities to the lowest common regulatory factor and ethical standard. Even if provinces succeed in fully harmonizing the rules to the highest common factor, they would still be subject to
Private Members' Business
different interpretations by different provincial regulators. This is why a federal regulator is needed to set national standards and to enforce these standards.
I am glad that my friend from Mississauga South is here. Not so long ago he was in full support of deregulating the financial institutions. We have pillars. Our system was built on pillars and we regulated the financial institutions by pillars; not pillars of salt, pillars. We had banks as one pillar. We had trust companies as another pillar. We had insurance companies as a third pillar. We had security brokerage houses as a fourth pillar.
In 1986 we knocked the brokerage houses down. That pillar went down. It probably saved a lot of them from bankruptcy. Immediately that pillar went down-
They are still there.
They were having some problems. Some of them were having problems. The member would admit that. Would my friend admit that?
They are still there.

The banks quickly moved in and bought the pillars, took the pillars over. Now each bank has a security brokerage pillar inside the stable. Of course we cannot have them communicating freely and openly so we put up Chinese walls. They call them Chinese walls. I call them picket fences because I think we can still move back and forward over them.
To some extent we have been cheating, have we not? We have been using a federal regulator, OSFI, through the back door. It is responsible for regulating banks and financial institutions and through the back door has been doing some regulation of brokerages.
Last year we completely knocked down the other pillars, all of them. They are all gone now. They are eating each other up as we predicted. Have you not seen it lately, Mr. Speaker? The banks are eating up the trust companies. The trust companies are going to be eaten up by insurance companies. Then the banks will eat up insurance companies because now banks can own insurance companies.

April 20,1993
Private Members' Business
If we extrapolate that, the banks can now own their own securities firms. Banks now have accounts combining bank stock and trading services. Bank trusts and insurance companies can offer investment counselling and portfolio management services without having to set up a subsidiary reporting to a provincial securities commission as was previously the case.
They are pushing this very lucrative, fee generating business. Since the regulation of banking, federally chartered insurance and trust companies falls on the federal jurisdiction, the federal regulator must be allowed to monitor the spectrum of activities. A strong federal presence is inevitable. It has to come.
I mentioned insider trader and I mentioned the Bennett-Doman case. It was a classic example of the inability to deal with an alleged problem because it spanned two jurisdictions, B.C. and Ontario. I would argue that my proposal would deal with problems like that one.
I would suggest that another reason for a national securities regulator is the fact that the federal government is already involved to some degree in securities regulation. Insider trading, takeover bid and other provisions of the Federal Business Corporations Act overlap provincial securities law. The Criminal Code includes provisions on stock manipulation and other forms of securities fraud. There is already some federal responsibility.
Another reason is more an argument to allay fears. It seems to me there are no significant constitutional impediments to an expansion of the federal government's role in security industry regulation. The federal trade and commerce power should impose sufficient authority to regulate securities trading.
I am not the only one who has argued for a national securities regulator. In the previous throne speech the Prime Minister put the following question: "Do we really need three separate securities regulators when all over the world countries are moving to a much more centralized regulatory regime?" It had even been included in the Charlottetown accord.
In terms of where we are headed that is what we have to do. I propose we should create a federal Canadian national securities exchange commission, CNSEC, along the lines of the Securities and Exchange Commission in
the United States. CNSEC would be run by an independent board of directors. I personally am not in favour of developing a parallel federal system of securities regulation. This would only it would seem to me add to the confusion to have a parallel federal system and a provincial one.
The mandate of this commission would be: one, to create an integrated national system of securities regulation, that is create one securities regulatory regime by integrating the provincial securities commission into CNSEC; two, I believe we should set accounting norms and technical and ethical standards for trading in securities which would be one of the functions of CNSEC; three, to supervise the sound and efficient functioning trade in securities, bonds and equities; four, to supervise the international flow of capital and investment into and out of Canada; five, investigate abuse and apply sanctions; six, to represent the national financial interests vis-a-vis the international forces currently working to create one global financial market.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Marc Robitaille (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, thank you for this opportunity to participate in this debate.
The motion before us today calls for the creation of a national securities regulator to address the issue of overlapping federal and provincial securities regulation.
I do not see the use for such an organization. The present system is working relatively well and is flexible enough. Why change so radically a system that is working?
April 20, 1993



Let me provide you, Mr. Speaker, with some background on this issue. Securities markets have traditionally been regulated by the provinces. Under the financial institution reform enacted last year most securities activities remain outside the business powers of federally-regulated financial institutions.
Even though there is a different regulatory regime in each province, the Canadian capital market works well. The provincial securities commissions co-ordinate their regulatory activities through the Canadian Securities Administrators.

I would like to point out that there is very little overlapping of federal and provincial securities regulations. When overlapping has occurred, discussions were held between the two levels of government to settle the matter.
The Hockin-Kwinter agreement for instance which was signed by the federal and Ontario governments in 1987 specified the division of powers and regulatory responsibility between the two levels of government with respect to securities.
The financial institutions legislation passed last year identified those securities transactions that federally chartered financial institutions could make. I understand that discussions on this issue are presently under way between the two levels of government.
The House will recall that the same legislation also reformed the statutory and regulatory framework for federally chartered financial institutions in Canada.
Barriers between the pillars of the financial sector, namely the banks, insurance companies and trust and loan companies, have been eliminated, allowing more direct competition between financial institutions.
The reform of financial institutions has benefited consumers through increased competition and a widening of the range of services provided by these institutions. The reform also increased the protection for depositors and insured persons and it strengthened the ability of Canadian financial institutions to compete here and abroad by providing them with new opportunities for growth. Banks, trust and loan companies, as well as insurance companies can now go outside their traditional sector and diversify their activity by owning institutions
Private Members' Business
in other fields of the financial services industry. For example, banks and insurance companies can own trust and loan companies; moreover, trust and loan companies as well as banks can own insurance companies. Thanks to this opportunity for diversification, financial institutions can now offer consumers a wider selection of goods and services.
The reform also gave greater powers to financial institutions. For example, trust and loan companies can enjoy the same internal powers as banks, including full authority to give credit to businesses and consumers. Also, insurance companies can now make loans to consumers and businesses.
Mr. Speaker, allow me to go back to the motion which is the subject of this debate. The federal government repeatedly said that it was committed to reducing duplication and overlapping.
Given the significant progress made regarding securities, and given the ability of the provinces to regulate this sector properly, I do not see the necessity of creating a national body to regulate the securities industry.
However I would like to take a moment to discuss more in detail the jurisdiction conflicts between the two levels of government, as well as some of the changes which have occurred in the eighties regarding the regulation of securities in Canada.
Given the importance of this industry for our economy, both the federal and the provincial governments are interested in establishing efficient securities markets.
I already said that in Canada these markets were traditionally regulated by the provinces. Provincial authorities are responsible for a good part of the day-today regulation of the securities markets.
As for the federal government, it looks at the internal operations on securities of federally chartered banks as well as trust and insurance companies. It also looks at the presence of foreign institutions on Canadian markets.

Further, the federal government is involved in the securities market through the takeover bid, insider trading disclosure and related provisions of the Canada Business Corporation Act. This act is administered by consumer and corporate affairs. The federal government

April 20, 1993
Private Members' Business
also has an interest in preserving the over-all efficient functioning of Canadian capital markets.

Both the federal government and the various provincial governments are involved in regulating certain aspects of the securities markets. However, responsibility is the operative word and responsibility lies mainly with the provinces.
Both levels of government agree that the basic division of supervisory responsibilities should not be modified. However, they acknowledge that problems have surfaced from time to time and that maintaining a system that works well requires considerable co-ordination and cooperation.
The federal government believes that by setting up a discussion process in which both levels of government would participate on an equal footing would be the best way to deal with the problems of overlapping and duplication. The changes we saw in the eighties with respect to the regulation of securities in Canada have shown the benefits of this approach.
The changes that took place on securities markets a few years ago have had two major effects on the sector. They promoted competition and encouraged international integration.
I would like to give a few examples of these changes and the effect they have had. When fixed commission rates on our main securities markets were either dropped or substantially reduced the industry started offering more competitive prices. The securities market expanded and became more sophisticated.
It seems I have only two minutes left. I will conclude my speech. There is a lot more I could say about the subject.
I have tried to provide a summary of what we have done to deal effectively with the pressures of competition by decompartmentalizing the securities industry, thanks to policy changes co-ordinated at the federal and provincial levels. That is something we must not forget.
We must remember that the changes in the securities industry were brought about thanks to the co-operation of both levels of government. Further changes would have to be made the same way.
The existing system in this country has worked well. If changes are necessary there are many ways to make these changes without modifying the existing federal and provincial framework. Unilaterally creating a national securities regulator would not fit in with this approach.
I therefore advise hon. members against supporting this motion.

Mr. Speaker,I would first like to compliment the hon. member for Nickel Belt with respect to the motion before us because it does illustrate some of the problems that we have been seeing in the subcommittee on financial institutions. I must say that I am disappointed to see that the representative from the government side is indicating a reluctance.
We saw in the number of things we looked at as we went through the financial institutions legislation a lot of overlap. We saw a lot of duplication. I will give an example of one situation. The Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation provides deposit insurance but because of provincial regulations on certain institutions it had to go to the provincial government first to request permission to go into that province to do something and to check out that particular institution. It seems to me that when you have a federal organization like the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation that you should have the right to go in and investigate to make sure that taxpayers' dollars as well as depositors' dollars are not in jeopardy.
We see this type of breakdown between provinces and the federal government in a number of areas dealing with the regulation of financial institutions.
We also see a situation in which the new legislation which has been introduced has created a new atmosphere, an atmosphere in which there is a blurring of the pillars within our financial institutions, and a competitiveness which we encourage. At the same time, as I am sure you will appreciate, Mr. Speaker, with competitiveness also comes a need to protect. Consumers have to be
April 20, 1993

protected, the systems have to be protected. We have to try to find that right balance. I believe that as we look at financial institutions and what is going on in that whole process, we must have what I would call national standards. This motion, which probably does not go far enough when you look at the over-all area of financial institutions, at least is a move in the right direction by having a regulator to deal with national securities types of situations.
We are in a global economy. We all recognize that. We also see what is happening in the European common market. We see where those financial institutions are going to be working in any of the different countries of the common market and they are going to have the same types of regulations and problems that we face in this country, but they are doing something about it by having national standards and, as far as the European common market is concerned, national regulations.
We are saying on this side that there is a need. We have OSFI which deals with some aspects of financial institutions but again, we in Parliament are concerned.
I know the chairman of the subcommittee is concerned because we are having difficulty getting information concerning the collapse of two trust companies. The Superintendent of Financial Institutions is taking the position that information should not be brought forward to our committee. There are things that need to be looked at and aired. There has to be at least a minimum standard in this country as far as securities are concerned but also with respect to all financial institutions.
We recognize of course that NAFTA is another aspect that is going to have implications on our financial institutions and where we go in that area. Again that is going to require us as a country to have strong national regulations. If we are going to be competitive in the international markets, which I believe we are, then at the same time we must have those protections so our financial institutions are sound. People who invest in our financial institutions and carry on business with them must have the security of knowing that those institutions are regulated and there are at least some minimum standards.
Private Members' Business
For that reason, as I have indicated, we feel there is an opportunity to go further with this particular motion and encompass some other aspects. I am hoping that our subcommittee of financial institutions will take on a supervisory role in the sense of looking at what has happened to a number of our financial institutions and determining for sure that the proper protections are in place.
We face a very critical test at this particular time with respect to finding out what went wrong with Central Trust and Standard Trust. There is a reluctance on the part of the superintendent to give us that information. It is my view that Parliament has a role to play here to make sure that those financial institutions are sound and Canadian taxpayers' dollars are in financially sound institutions.
If we carry this motion one step further and provide a regulatory oversight dealing with national securities matters, I think a regulatory oversight with Parliament involved in the process is also a proper direction for us to be taking. In that sense our committee must exert its influence in making sure the demands for information from OSFI are brought forward.
I think the motion put forward goes in that direction to some degree, but as indicated earlier I do not believe it goes far enough.
I would also say that listening to the government's position, it looked at all sorts of different pieces of legislation and all sorts of different bodies that are regulating one aspect or another of financial institutions. If we are going to harmonize the things that are going on in this country in the area of financial institutions, we have to consolidate them under one or two regulatory agencies rather than have this proliferation of different agencies looking at different aspects of our financial institutions.
I think that is the thrust, in part, of this particular motion. In that regard we are supportive of the direction and concept, but recognize that in typical fashion the NDP members have not gone far enough. They are hesitant and timid in their approach. As the chairman of the subcommittee has said, they are the lackeys of big banks and big banking institutions and therefore are reluctant to really jump into this and do the job properly.

April 20, 1993
Private Members' Business

Mr. Speaker, I want to say I am very pleased to join the debate today and I am delighted that my friend from Nickel Belt has brought this motion forward. I think the motion cuts to the heart of one of the major problems we have in this country. When we started as a country at Confederation we had different banks in different parts of the country issuing the currency. We did not have a national currency and we did not have national markets.
As a consequence, issues like security, trading and so on became under the purview of the provinces. For a long time the whole concept of judging the validity of securities, what is in a security, how it is regulated and who can sell securities has been a matter of provincial jurisdiction.
I suppose that was fine as long as a security dealer only raised money from the local community to start a business in the local community where the security dealer was. It was perfectly fine. So we developed stock markets in Toronto and Montreal and security dealers operated in those markets. By and large those markets dealt with companies that dealt only in Canada. They floated issues for Canadians wanting to raise money to build enterprises in Canada.
After a while new markets were developed in western Canada and we developed stock markets in Vancouver and Calgary. Alberta and British Columbia also developed detailed security regulations.
The other provinces of course developed security regulation systems to deal with the registration of non-transferrable securities and debentures.
The trouble is that we are growing and the world is growing and our dollar is traded today in every market in the world, 24 hours a day.
It used to be that the Minister of Finance would not read a budget until eight o'clock at night after all the markets had closed. Today it does not matter when he reads the budget because there are markets trading our securities everywhere in the world. In a sense we ought to have some sort of world regulator of these institutions, but that is not possible so at least we should have something done nationally.
It is a matter of constitutional negotiation. It was at the Charlottetown accord group and was not dealt with there. It should have been dealt with there.
Dealing with trust companies, for example, we have a situation where provinces regulate these companies and so we had the obscene situation in the province of Alberta where the province licensed Principal Trust. Principal Trust could not get a licence to operate in Ontario because the Ontario regulators smelled a rat. It could not get a licence to operate in Quebec because the Quebec regulators smelled a rat, so it operated in British Columbia, Nova Scotia and Newfoundland where it got registered. People lost their shirts in those provinces because there was no over-all regulation. They thought they were depositing with Principal Trust which was covered by CDIC when they were in fact buying a Principal land deal or a Principal mutual fund or a Principal somewhere else and getting no principal back. That is the problem with securities.
We saw the Bennett-Doman case brought forward by my friend where fast and loose action was pretty much condescended to in Vancouver but objected to in Toronto, so no satisfactory result came in that matter.
We cannot run a country with markets that are designed to raise money for national and international projects and a market system that is supposed to handle the trades of securities issued in other jurisdictions if we do not run those markets on a national and consolidated basis.
There is no great advantage to a province in regulating securities. It always shocks me that provincial treasurers see the regulation of securities as something they ought to keep together and close at hand. They think that perhaps if they keep the security business in their province they will somehow attract money into the province.
We have seen the kind of money they attract. They attract the bad deals because the bad deals which cannot be registered elsewhere go to where the regulation is the softest and where the regulation is the softest we wind up with the frauds and with the wash trading. We wind up with the fast dealers and with Canada receiving a bad reputation as a place where people can invest their funds.
We need a lot of funds in this country. We have a big country to build. We have needs for massive amounts of investment and we cannot raise all of that investment here. We have to raise it around the world. We cannot raise investment around the world when we continue to threaten investors with sloppy and incompetent regula-
April 20, 1993

tion that has existed in at least two of the markets in this country.
A myriad of regulators.

My hon. friend from Nickel Belt says a myriad of regulators.
It is about time that we rationalize this business. It is about time that the governments of this country recognized the fact that there is no merit in soft and sloppy regulation. Soft and sloppy regulation hurts everyone in Canada and does not give the province that facilitates soft and sloppy regulation any advantage at all.
You do not make any marks by having your citizens get burned. You do not get any marks by having other people's citizens get burned because they remember and they will not be back.
I say that this resolution has a great deal of merit to it. Does it go far enough? Does it do the right thing? I certainly say that it does not because it really is not a question of duplication. It is a question that security regulation is virtually, totally and completely a provincial matter. We really have no federal security regulator at all. While the federal government may regulate the banks that have security licences, indirectly in that sense it controls the solvency of the banks. It does not control how the security operations are conducted, how registration is conducted or what prospectuses say and so on.
All of these very important matters are not regulated nationally. What we have is a situation where we have only provincial regulations. Really if this resolution had been corrected, it would have said that we instruct the federal government to immediately start negotiations with the provinces to reorganize this Confederation and take over certain things that really ought to be national.
We do a lot of things here nationally that ought to be provincial. There is no reason whatsoever why we have a federal Department of Forestry. There is no reason whatsoever why we have a federal housing minister. Absolutely not.
Housing for example, foolish. We cannot subdivide land here. We cannot organize building permits here. We cannot direct housing regulation here. We cannot do anything in the housing market. We ought to leave the housing market to the provinces. They can do it. We are not needed here. But we are needed where the real
Private Members' Business
problems are in this countiy and those real problems are in the money markets of this world where we have a Canadian dollar, Canadian securities, Canadian opportunities and we ought to make sure that those opportunities are governed, directed, controlled and developed in a national system.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to take a few minutes to speak on this motion.
I commend the motion to the House and I congratulate the member who put it forward.
The member for Mississauga South says perhaps the resolution should have read that the federal government be empowered or something like that or directed to consult with the provinces and so on in regard to creating the office of the national securities regulator. I suppose there are many ways in which one can make any motion better than it was originally drafted. That is not the point.
The motion when passed will I assume become the subject matter of deliberations in a committee. The committee is not restricted to doing precisely and only the things that are written in the motion. The committee looking into the issue subsequently could broaden that mandate and obviously do that which the member for Mississauga South asks.
In addition it is implicit in the motion in any case that if there is overlapping at the present time, and if we were to eliminate overlapping particularly in an area that involves provincial jurisdictions, we would have to consult the jurisdiction which is presently charged with that in order to eliminate the overlapping. The argument of the member for Mississauga South is not quite accurate, I say respectfully. I know the member for Mississauga South who is listening very closely to this debate now that he has finished his remarks will take note of that.
The member for Mississauga South said a number of things that I agree with nevertheless. When talking about such things as trust companies and the way they are registered at the present time and the fact that different provinces have different rules involving trust

April 20, 1993
Private Members' Business
companies, most Canadians investing right now in trust companies do not know whether the trust company they are investing in is federally or provincially chartered and regulated. It is not obvious at all at the present time which ones get their directions from which agency of government. That is just one example.
Notwithstanding this there is still a need to ensure or to at least attempt to provide if not guidance, if that word is too strong, then at the very least co-ordination so that there would be at the federal level at least a repository of the different rules that apply in each province so that provinces can attempt to have rules that are similar.
I will use another example to make a parallel. Inside the Department of the Secretary of State there is an agency-I forget the name of it for the moment-which is charged with co-ordinating educational programs. We all know of course that education is strictly the prerogative of the provincial level of government. Nevertheless, the Secretary of State I believe has an official there or at least a group within that department and the purpose of this group is to co-ordinate as best it can. I know the members are going to say it is not nearly co-ordinated enough because there are still vast differences between the educational standards in various jurisdictions in Canada. Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, you will understand what I am indicating to you here, namely that such agencies exist at the present time to co-ordinate provincial power in Canada or co-ordinate areas which fall under provincial jurisdiction.
Just as what we said is true in the area of education, and the member for Mississauga South indicated it is equally true in the area of regulating the trust industiy, it is also true in the securities industry generally.
Without putting too fine a point on it, stock exchanges in this country are not exactly the same in terms of how they deal with certain speculative ventures and the like. A particular province seems to have made quite an industry. It is into more speculative stock than other jurisdictions, which is fine I suppose. However, if we were at least sure that the way in which we measure these things is uniform across the country then investors would be better assured that when they take a risk on more speculative stock they would be doing so with the
full knowledge that the rule by which the level of risk is measured is uniform everywhere.
I see nothing wrong with having this motion adopted by this House, sent to a parliamentary committee and there amended and corrected. At the very least we should provide for some co-ordination between the various provincial jurisdictions in Canada.
There is a wider debate in all of this. The member for Mississauga South raised the issue of whether or not some provincial powers should now be federal and federal powers should now be provincial and so on. After the debacle of the Charlottetown agreement last fall I am not sure that Canadians are willing to get into a very heavy debate of this kind at this time. In the future these things will inevitably come up again. If we wait for the next round of constitutional negotiations before we address any of these issues we will probably wait a very long time.

Meanwhile, I do not see why we should not proceed with this motion, why it should not be passed by the House and referred to a Parliamentary committee which could, at the very least, enable us to try and implement some of the principles or some of the proposals made today by the hon. member for Nickel Belt.

speakeroldname: Mr. Andre Harvey (Parliamentary Secretary to Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not surprised that the New Democratic Party would make such a proposal because I must say, with all due respect for my friend from the NDP and those who support him, they always seem to go against the flow and in this case against the new pattern responsible governments are trying to develop.
In 1984, we realized that we could not go on setting up new agencies for the benefit of the regime's friends. What we implemented was a new system based on what we called privatization.
Since 1984 privatization has meant the disappearance of scores of Crown agencies or corporations, with some 90,000 employees assigned unproductive tasks. The result was that instead of increasing by 14.8 per cent a year, as was the case before, spending increased only by 3 per cent to 4 per cent a year. This is very significant, because if spending had continued to increase at a rate of 15 per cent a year, we would have a debt of $850 billion instead of $450 billion, and the deficit would reach $82 billion
April 20, 1993

this year instead of $34 billion. Technically we would be bankrupt. Clearly, the example not to follow is Ontario, where the deficit has tripled.
With these proposals, we would be interfering in provincial jurisdictions. There is close co-operation between the various levels of government in the area of securities-as in many other areas-and doing away with all trade barriers between provinces is an excessively important goal of our government. We will try to finalize within a year a free trade agreement encompassing virtually all areas of the Canadian economy to have the same openness between provinces we now enjoy with the United States and will shortly enjoy with Mexico.
In conclusion, this proposal seems to me totally unacceptable as it goes against streamlining and spending control.

Mr. Speaker, on March 11 I asked the Prime Minister of Canada to tell us why his government was refraining from tabling a budget and showing Canadians the real financial situation of our country.
The Conservatives often say they want to present to Canadians, on a regular basis, a budget depicting the real economic state of our country. For partisan reasons only,
Adjournment Debate
the Minister of Finance has decided to break that promise this year so that candidates for the leadership of the Conservative Party are not embarrassed by a somewhat tighter budget.
To hear candidates for the leadership of the Conservative Party talk non-stop about how they will reduce the annual deficit of the Conservative government, freeze taxes, cut government expenditures, et cetera, is absolutely absurd. One has to wonder why these people, who in some cases have two, three or four years of experience as members of the cabinet, did not share their ideas with their government before. Why did they keep their views to themselves and wait for a leadership campaign to disclose them? We wonder about that.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: They did not think about it.

They did not think about it, as the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell said.
Did all those bright ideas come to them as soon as the Prime Minister announced he was quitting? We have to wonder. Could it be that the candidates are coming up with all those ideas only to impress Canadians in preelection time? You only have to recall all the broken promises made by the Conservative government during the last two election campaigns to realize how weak its commitments are.
Our country is in deep financial trouble and this is not a game of Monopoly. It is the duty of the Conservative government to advise Parliament of its plans, objectives, policies and the economic future of our country.
During the last nine years the Conservative government has doubled Canada's public debt to the appalling level of $450 billion. At a time when some provinces are working wonders to minimize the negative impact of the cuts in federal transfer payments, Conservative leadership candidates are standing by a project as indefensible and as extravagant as the purchase of helicopters at a cost of $5.8 billion.
It is important to know if the government will keep going on and develop other projects as crazy as this one which drain such important programs as social, education and health programs, or if it will finally invest its energy in stimulating the economy and give back some hope to the 1,537,000 unemployed and 2.3 million people on welfare.

April 20, 1993
Adjournment Debate
The government had indicated that a budget would be tabled in the week following the Easter recess. This is now and we have no budget. We do not even have a date when it will be presented. Until now no date has been set and it does seem to have as a priority to set one. Although we cannot expect much from a government such as the one we now have and that is driving the country into bankruptcy, we will at the very least have the chance to know the truth about the financial situation if the government summons the courage to table a budget for Canadians, a budget that could boost our economy.
I repeat the question I asked the Prime Minister a few weeks ago: What is the exact date of the budget we are to get in order to really know the true face of the Conservative government policy and also the country's financial situation so that we can correct it after the next election?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 15 I asked the Minister of Employment and Immigration to do two things: first, to table amendments to the Immigration Act in order to make gender persecution a specific ground for refugee status and, second, to admit those women into Canada who had been victims of gender persecution but turned down by the Immigration Refugee Board before the new guidelines of March 19, 1993.
Under the present law and the international treaty on refugees, a refugee is defined as a person who has a well founded fear of persecution for reasons of race, religion, nationality, membership in a social group or political opinion. Gender is not included in the definition although there are situations in the world where, first, women are by law relegated to an inferior position and prohibited from doing certain things and are persecuted if they disobey such laws. Second, women in many countries are not protected by the law from personal maltreatment, abuse and violence. Third, where women are subject to persecution as I have described, if they speak out or campaign against such laws they are persecuted as well.
On March 9 the chairperson of the Immigration and Refugee Board issued instructions to the Immigration and Refugee Board members that they should interpret the definition of refugee to consider gender persecution. She said on that occasion that these instructions were not binding and that the gender persecution was not to be a ground of refugee status in itself but must be linked to one of the existing grounds such as race or religion and so on.
It is for these reasons I asked the minister on March 25 to go one step further to make gender a distinct ground for refugee status and make it binding by putting it in the law. The minister answered on that day that he could not do it because it would go beyond the international convention on refugees. To that I say that the convention is only a floor, not a ceiling. Nothing prevents Canada from having a larger, more generous definition of a refugee, but we cannot do less than the convention we have signed.
April 20, 1993

I have also asked the minister to admit on a humanitarian and compassionate basis those victims of gender persecution who were rejected by the board before the new instructions were promulgated. I understand there are over 35 such cases.
In conclusion, I would hope that the government would respond to this request in a more positive manner because I know many Canadians would support such a policy.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Belsher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for raising this question once again with us.
I want to tell the hon. member that the guidelines on gender based persecutions issued by the chairperson of the Immigration and Refugee Board on March 9 are intended to promote consistency in decisions of refugee claims. They are consistent with the interpretation of the definition of a convention refugee proposed in the 1985 resolution of the executive committee of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees which Canada supported. This allows decision makers to consider women refugee claimants as members of a social group.
These guidelines were the first issued pursuant to the authority of the chairperson contained in recent amendments to the Immigration Act, Bill C-86. There is no reason to believe these non-binding guidelines that respect the independence of decision makers and that were developed in a consultative process will be less effective in promoting consistency than binding direction on the interpretation of the convention definition.
Persecution against a woman based on any one of the five grounds delineated in the refugee convention can result in that woman being recognized as a refugee. If the persecution is solely the consequence of the fact that the individual is a woman or is directed against a particular subgroup of women, the claim can be accepted on the basis that she is a member of a particular social group. The process of evaluation of a refugee claim would not be any easier if the definition of a convention refugee were amended either within Canada or internationally to include gender.
I hope this answers the member's concerns.
Adjournment Debate CHILD PORNOGRAPHY

Mr. Speaker, tonight I am standing before my colleagues in the House of Commons to discuss once again the issue of pornography and the urgent need for legislation to outlaw the possession of pornographic materials.
When I last discussed this issue in the House in December I was assured by the Minister of Justice that child pornography legislation would be introduced early this year. Since we now have a new justice minister I would like to know whether introducing this legislation is a priority for the new minister.
Hard core pornography degrades the women and children who are portrayed in these submissive, subordinate and often violent pictures. These videos, magazines and pictures demean our entire society.
We currently have laws that make it an offence to produce, manufacture and sell pornography in Canada. Last February the Supreme Court ruled on pornography in the Butler case. This case concerned obscenity provisions in the Criminal Code. The Supreme Court decision upheld the existing obscenity provisions. The Butler ruling is an important one. In it Canada's highest court has recognized what women and many concerned Canadians have been saying for years. The Supreme Court has acknowledged the harm that pornography's demeaning and dehumanizing depictions of sex can cause to society in general and to women and children in particular. The Butler decision was also important in that it expanded the scope of the existing anti-obscenity law which referred to child pornography.
Pornography is a dangerous and degrading weapon being used in the war against women and children. It reflects the perception that women and children are inferior and available to service the sexual needs of men.
As elected officials we must make sure that legislation is introduced in the area of possession of pornography. We must also make sure that the existing legislation which outlaws the production, sale and manufacturing of pornography is effectively enforced.
In closing I want to say that as a society we have been far too tolerant of pornography. We have the facts. We see the images of young children and women who are our mothers, daughters and granddaughters being beaten, raped and murdered. We have read the evidence showing the link between hard core pornography and the

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member from Markham has asked the government to address the very urgent need to create an offence for the possession of child pornography, and the government could not agree with the hon. member more.
Let me assure the hon. member that the Minister of Justice recognizes the need to prohibit the production and possession of child pornography to protect children from the harmful effects of sexual abuse and sexual exploitation.
The minister convened more than 250 people at a national symposium on community safety and crime prevention which was held in Toronto in March and clearly indicated that it is his intention to introduce measures in this Elouse as soon as possible which will specifically prohibit the possession, production, distribution and sale of child pornography. This will be done in the very near future.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George-Bulkley Valley):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, back on December 9 I had the opportunity to question the minister of trade on a very important trade matter between Canada and the United States, specifically the softwood lumber tariff dispute.
My question at that time concerned news reports that information on the review of this dispute by the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade had been made public, in particular that GATT had made a split decision on the softwood dispute. On the one hand it had ruled that the United States, while using special procedures to launch this harassment, this countervail action against our softwood exports, was proper in doing so. On the other hand it ruled in Canada's favour on the question of whether the United States was right in its continuing to collect the 15 per cent lumber export surcharge or tariff that our own government and country had disavowed. I asked the minister that day in the House to confirm
whether this was in fact correct and the news reports were right from GATT that it was dealing with this particular issue. I wanted also to pursue this question. If in fact the ruling had come down as it did and the United States and its officials owed Canadians some $15 million, what kind of assurances and what kind of work was the government going to do to ensure that we would get our money back?
I understand now from discussions that my staff have had with officials that the GATT subsidy committee will be meeting on April 28 to officially review this case. I hope that the government in responding will give an indication of the success that we have had to date in getting our $15 million back and also the direction that we can expect and what preparations the government has for the eventual decision from GATT and of course the ongoing panels on subsidy and injury that are dealing with this issue.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Dorothy Dobbie (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Minister of State (Agriculture)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Agriculture)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we will respond to the question the hon. member asked in the first place. I am delighted to do so and to clarify the GATT report on the U.S. actions against softwood lumber exports in Canada.
The report contains two major findings. First, it found that the U.S. was not justified under the GATT subsidies code to have placed temporary bans on imports of softwood lumber from Canada between October 4, 1991 and March 12, 1992.
The panel has therefore recommended to the subsidies committee that the U.S. refund the cash collected as a result of this action. Second, Canada challenged the initiation of the investigation in the first place. However, the panel found that the Department of Commerce had met the standard for sufficient evidence toward the initiation of countervailing duty investigation into provincial stumpage pricing practices.
Notwithstanding this, the panel specifically noted that it was not deciding whether Canadian stumpage pricing practices were in fact subsidies.
Also raised was the question of whether the GATT panel made a decision with regard to Canada's export of raw logs. The panel found this issue to be outside its terms of reference even though we pressed to have the issue addressed.
April 20, 1993

Finally, the question of access to the U.S. market for our softwood lumber producers is of course of very great importance. Canada is contesting the final decisions of the U.S. on subsidy and injury on Canadian softwood lumber through two chapter nineteen panels established under the free trade agreement.
We are also examining the option of pursuing the softwood lumber case further in the GATT.
